uz.earliestSettlement: Samarkand is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Central Asia, settled by at least the 7th century BC.

keyDates.event: Alexander the Great conquers Sogdiana, including Samarkand
Sogdian merchants rise as leading traders along the Silk Road (approx.)
Arab conquest of Transoxiana begins the Islamization of the region
Samanid dynasty established, with Bukhara flourishing as a center of Islamic learning
Genghis Khan's Mongol army destroys Bukhara and Samarkand
Timur (Tamerlane) makes Samarkand the capital of his empire
Ulugh Beg builds his observatory in Samarkand, advancing astronomy
Uzbek Shaybanid dynasty founds the Khanate of Bukhara
Khanate of Kokand emerges as a separate state alongside Bukhara and Khiva
Russian Empire captures Tashkent
Emirate of Bukhara becomes a Russian protectorate
Uzbek SSR formed within the Soviet Union
Stalinist purges devastate the Uzbek SSR's political and cultural leadership
Independence from the Soviet Union, September 1
Andijan unrest and crackdown
Shavkat Mirziyoyev becomes president, launching a reform era

uz.climate: Mostly arid continental desert/steppe, hot summers and cold winters.
funFacts: Tashkent's metro, opened in 1977, was the first in Central Asia - and its stations are famous for lavish, palace-like decoration.
Samarkand's Registan Square has stood as a public square for roughly 600 years.
Uzbekistan is one of only two 'doubly landlocked' countries in the world (the other is Liechtenstein) - meaning it's landlocked by other landlocked countries.
The Silk Road ran directly through Uzbekistan, making Bukhara and Samarkand major trading hubs for over a thousand years.
Plov has regional variants across the country - Samarkand's version differs from Tashkent's and Fergana's.
Uzbekistan is one of the world's leading cotton exporters, and cotton has long been central to its economy, earning it the nickname 'white gold.'
The Aral Sea, once one of the world's four largest lakes, has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s due to Soviet-era irrigation diversions, with much of its former bed inside Uzbekistan.
Uzbekistan became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991.
Khiva's walled inner city, Itchan Kala, was the first site in Uzbekistan to be inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Uzbek has been written in the Latin alphabet since a transition from Cyrillic began in the 1990s.
Samarkand was one of the great cities of the ancient Silk Road and later became the capital of Timur's empire.
Uzbekistan is a major producer of natural gas and gold.
Navruz, the Persian New Year celebrated at the spring equinox, is one of Uzbekistan's most important traditional holidays.

kz.earliestSettlement: The Botai culture, in northern Kazakhstan, is associated with some of the earliest evidence of horse domestication, around 3500 BC.

keyDates.event: Kazakh Khanate founded
Beginning of Russian imperial expansion into Kazakh lands
Russia founds Verny, a military outpost later renamed Almaty
Soviet collectivization causes a devastating famine (Asharshylyq) that kills over a million Kazakhs
Kazakh SSR established
Jeltoqsan protests erupt in Almaty against Soviet rule
Independence from the Soviet Union, December 16
Capital moved from Almaty to Akmola, soon renamed Astana
Astana renamed Nur-Sultan, then reverted to Astana in 2022
'Bloody January' unrest - mass protests over fuel prices met with a deadly crackdown

kz.climate: Continental, with hot summers and very cold winters; semi-arid to arid in the south.

unesco.name: Saryarka – Steppe and Lakes of Northern Kazakhstan

funFacts: Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country by area.
The Baikonur Cosmodrome, leased to Russia, is the world's first and largest operational space launch facility - it's where Yuri Gagarin launched into orbit.
Kazakhstan is believed to be where horses were first domesticated, roughly 5,500 years ago.
Almaty means 'father of apples' - the wild ancestor of the domestic apple, Malus sieversii, originated in the mountains near the city.
Kazakhstan voluntarily gave up the world's fourth-largest nuclear arsenal after independence in the 1990s.
Kazakhstan moved its capital from Almaty to Astana in 1997.
Baikonur Cosmodrome is still used today to launch crewed missions to the International Space Station.
The Caspian Sea, the world's largest inland body of water, borders western Kazakhstan.
Kazakhstan is the ninth-largest country in the world by land area.

tj.earliestSettlement: Sarazm, a proto-urban settlement near Panjakent, dates back to around 4000 BC.

keyDates.event: Samanid Empire flourishes, centered on Bukhara, regarded as the Tajik golden age (approx.)
Russian Empire establishes a protectorate over the Bukhara Emirate
Tajik Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic created within the Uzbek SSR
Tajik SSR separated from the Uzbek SSR
Independence from the Soviet Union, September 9
Civil war begins, lasting until 1997
Peace agreement ends the Tajik Civil War

tj.climate: Continental, strongly varied by elevation - hot lowlands, alpine Pamir highlands.

unesco.name: Tajik National Park (Mountains of the Pamirs)

funFacts: The Nurek Dam was, for decades, the tallest dam in the world.
Over 90% of Tajikistan is mountainous, most of it part of the Pamir and Alay ranges.
The Pamirs are nicknamed the 'Roof of the World'.
Tajik is a form of Persian, making Tajikistan the only Persian-speaking country in Central Asia.
The Pamir Highway, which crosses Tajikistan, is one of the highest international roads in the world.
Lake Karakul, high in the Tajik Pamirs, sits in a crater believed to have been formed by a meteorite impact around 25 million years ago.
Tajikistan's mountain rivers give it enormous hydropower potential, a key resource for its economy.
The ruins of Penjikent, an ancient Silk Road city in Tajikistan, preserve remains of pre-Islamic Sogdian civilization and are sometimes called the 'Pompeii of Central Asia.'

kg.earliestSettlement: The Sulaiman-Too mountain in Osh has been a place of worship and settlement for over 3,000 years.

keyDates.event: Russian Empire annexes the Kokand Khanate, incorporating Kyrgyz lands
Kara-Kyrgyz Autonomous Oblast established within Soviet Russia
Kirghiz SSR established
Osh riots - deadly ethnic violence between Kyrgyz and Uzbeks
Independence from the Soviet Union, August 31
Tulip Revolution ousts President Akayev
Second revolution leads to a parliamentary system of government
Renewed ethnic violence erupts in Osh and Jalal-Abad
October Revolution protests overturn a disputed election, bringing Sadyr Japarov to power

kg.climate: Continental and strongly mountainous, with sharp altitude-driven variation.
funFacts: Lake Issyk-Kul is the second-largest alpine lake in the world after Titicaca, and it never freezes despite the surrounding snow.
The Epic of Manas, Kyrgyzstan's national epic poem, is one of the longest epic poems in the world - far longer than the Iliad and Odyssey combined.
Kyrgyzstan is sometimes called the 'Switzerland of Central Asia' because over 90% of its territory is mountainous.
Kyrgyzstan is home to the ancient nomadic tradition of eagle hunting, in which hunters train golden eagles to catch prey.
Kok-boru, a traditional horseback game in which riders compete to place a goat carcass in a goal, remains popular across Kyrgyzstan.
Bishkek, the capital, was known as Frunze during the Soviet era.
Yurts, traditional felt tents, are still widely used by nomadic herders in Kyrgyzstan's summer mountain pastures.
Kyrgyzstan became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991.
The Tian Shan mountain range, meaning 'Celestial Mountains,' covers much of Kyrgyzstan and is shared with China and Kazakhstan.
Kumis, fermented mare's milk, is a traditional Kyrgyz drink with deep roots in nomadic life.
kg.territorialNote: Kyrgyzstan has unresolved border areas with Tajikistan in the Fergana Valley, which have led to periodic armed clashes.

tm.earliestSettlement: Ancient Merv, one of the great oasis-cities of the Silk Road, has roots going back over 2,500 years.

keyDates.event: Merv flourishes as a major Silk Road city and Seljuk capital (approx.)
Mongols destroy Merv, killing much of its population
Russian Empire conquers the region at the Battle of Geok Tepe
Turkmen SSR established
Independence from the Soviet Union, October 27
UN recognizes Turkmenistan's permanent neutrality
President Saparmurat Niyazov dies after ruling since independence

tm.climate: Mostly arid desert (Karakum Desert covers ~70% of the country).

unesco.name: State Historical and Cultural Park 'Ancient Merv'

funFacts: Turkmenistan's Darvaza Gas Crater has been burning continuously since the 1970s.
Turkmenistan is one of the world's most sparsely populated countries relative to its land area - the Karakum Desert covers most of the country.
The Akhal-Teke, Turkmenistan's national horse breed, is famous for its metallic sheen and appears on the national emblem.
Ashgabat holds a Guinness World Record for the highest concentration of white marble buildings of any city in the world.
Turkmenistan possesses some of the largest natural gas reserves on Earth, centered on the massive Galkynysh field.
The ancient Silk Road city of Merv, now in ruins in Turkmenistan, was once one of the largest cities in the world before being destroyed by the Mongols in the 13th century.
Turkmenistan declared permanent neutrality, formally recognized by the United Nations in 1995, which remains a cornerstone of its foreign policy.
Ashgabat's Alem Cultural and Entertainment Center houses a Guinness World Record holder for the largest indoor Ferris wheel.
tm.currencyNote: Turkmenistan redenominated its currency in 2009, introducing a new manat worth 5,000 old manat.

us.earliestSettlement: Indigenous peoples inhabited North America for over 15,000 years before European colonization; the earliest lasting European colony was St. Augustine, Florida (1565).

keyDates.event: Jamestown founded, the first permanent English colony in North America
Mayflower Pilgrims land at Plymouth
Declaration of Independence
US Constitution drafted
Louisiana Purchase roughly doubles the size of the United States
Mexican-American War ends; US gains vast Southwest territories
American Civil War begins
Slavery abolished (13th Amendment)
Spanish-American War ends; US gains overseas territories
United States enters World War I
Wall Street Crash triggers the Great Depression
Pearl Harbor attack brings the US into World War II
End of World War II; US emerges as a global superpower
Civil Rights Act outlaws segregation and discrimination
Apollo 11 moon landing
September 11 terrorist attacks

us.climate: Extremely varied: arctic in Alaska, tropical in Hawaii/Florida, arid in the Southwest, temperate elsewhere.
funFacts: The United States has no official national language at the federal level.
Alaska is both the westernmost and, because the Aleutian Islands cross the 180th meridian, technically the easternmost US state.
The Hoover Dam used enough concrete to pave a two-lane road from San Francisco to New York.
The United States is the third-largest country in the world by both land area and population.
The Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776, a date celebrated annually as the country's national day.
The US Constitution, ratified in 1788, is the oldest surviving written national constitution still in force.
The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France, dedicated in New York Harbor in 1886.
Thomas Edison held over 1,000 US patents, including for the practical incandescent light bulb.
The Wright brothers achieved the first sustained, powered airplane flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903.
Yellowstone, established in 1872, was the world's first national park.
Basketball was invented in 1891 by James Naismith, a physical education teacher in Springfield, Massachusetts.
Apollo 11 made the first crewed Moon landing in 1969, with astronaut Neil Armstrong the first person to walk on the lunar surface.

gb.earliestSettlement: Settlement in Britain dates back to the Paleolithic; London itself was founded by the Romans as Londinium around 43 AD.

keyDates.event: Julius Caesar's first expedition to Britain
Roman conquest of Britain begins under Emperor Claudius
St Augustine's mission brings Christianity to Anglo-Saxon England
Viking raid on Lindisfarne marks the start of Norse invasions
Norman Conquest of England
Magna Carta signed
Black Death arrives, killing roughly a third of the population
Act of Supremacy establishes the Church of England under Henry VIII
Royal Navy defeats the Spanish Armada
English Civil War begins
Acts of Union create the Kingdom of Great Britain
Act of Union with Ireland forms the United Kingdom
Slavery Abolition Act ends slavery across most of the British Empire
Britain enters the First World War
WWII ends; postwar decolonization begins
UK joins the European Economic Community
UK formally leaves the European Union (Brexit)

gb.climate: Temperate maritime - mild, often cloudy and rainy.
funFacts: The United Kingdom is made up of four nations: England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
The London Underground, opened in 1863, is the oldest underground railway network in the world.
Big Ben is technically the name of the bell, not the clock tower.
The UK has no single written constitution, relying instead on acts of Parliament, legal precedent, and long-standing conventions.
Stonehenge, in Wiltshire, is a prehistoric monument whose massive stones were transported from as far as Wales, hundreds of kilometres away.
Fish and chips became a beloved national dish in the 19th century, combining fried fish with fried potatoes.
Modern codified versions of football, rugby, cricket, tennis, and golf all trace their rules to Britain.
The Beatles, who formed in Liverpool, became one of the best-selling and most influential bands in music history.
Buckingham Palace, the monarch's London residence, has 775 rooms.
The UK consists of over 6,000 islands in addition to the island of Great Britain.
William Shakespeare, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language, was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564.
The Channel Tunnel, opened in 1994, links England and France and contains one of the longest undersea sections of any tunnel in the world.

ru.earliestSettlement: The Kievan Rus' state, the earliest East Slavic state, was founded around 882 AD.

keyDates.event: Founding of Kievan Rus'
Vladimir the Great adopts Orthodox Christianity as the state religion
Mongol invasion of Rus' begins
Great Stand on the Ugra River ends Mongol rule over Muscovy
Ivan IV crowned first Tsar of Russia
Romanov dynasty begins with Michael I
Peter the Great founds St. Petersburg
Napoleon's invasion of Russia is repelled
Emancipation of the serfs
Russian Revolution; end of the monarchy
Soviet Union formally established
Soviet Union helps defeat Nazi Germany in WWII
Yuri Gagarin becomes the first human in space
Dissolution of the Soviet Union
Russia annexes Crimea
Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine

ru.climate: Vast range from subarctic/tundra in Siberia to humid continental and subtropical in the south.
ru.nationalSport: Bandy (official); ice hockey is most popular
funFacts: Russia spans 11 time zones, more than any other country.
Lake Baikal holds about 20% of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water - more than all five North American Great Lakes combined.
The Trans-Siberian Railway is the longest railway line in the world, spanning over 9,289 km.
Russia is the largest country in the world by land area, spanning nearly twice the area of Canada, the second-largest.
The Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, housed in the former Winter Palace, holds more than three million works of art and artifacts.
Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's ballets 'The Nutcracker' and 'Swan Lake' remain among the most performed in the world.
The Soviet Union, Russia's predecessor state, launched the first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, in 1957, and sent the first human, Yuri Gagarin, into space in 1961.
The Moscow Metro is famed for its ornate, palace-like stations, many built with chandeliers, mosaics and marble.
Oymyakon in Siberian Russia is considered one of the coldest permanently inhabited places on Earth.
Matryoshka nesting dolls, Russia's iconic folk craft, were first made in the late 19th century, inspired by Japanese nesting figures.
ru.currencyNote: Russia redenominated its currency in 1998, replacing 1,000 old rubles with 1 new ruble after the hyperinflation of the 1990s.
ru.territorialNote: Russia's borders include areas of dispute, most notably Crimea, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014 and administers, but which most of the international community continues to recognize as part of Ukraine.

cn.earliestSettlement: Chinese civilization along the Yellow River dates back over 5,000 years; the Shang Dynasty (c. 1600 BC) left the earliest confirmed written records.

keyDates.event: Shang Dynasty begins, China's earliest dynasty with written records
Zhou Dynasty established
Qin Shi Huang unifies China, becomes first emperor
Han Dynasty founded, the Silk Road trade routes open
Tang Dynasty founded, a golden age of culture and trade
Song Dynasty founded, noted for gunpowder and printing innovations
Mongol-led Yuan Dynasty established
Ming Dynasty founded; construction of the Forbidden City begins
Admiral Zheng He begins his treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean
Qing Dynasty founded by the Manchus
First Opium War with Britain begins, ending in the cession of Hong Kong (1842)
Qing Dynasty falls; Republic of China founded
Second Sino-Japanese War begins
People's Republic of China proclaimed
Cultural Revolution begins
Economic reforms under Deng Xiaoping begin
Tiananmen Square protests
Hong Kong returned to Chinese sovereignty

cn.climate: Extremely varied: monsoon in the southeast, arid in the northwest, alpine on the Tibetan Plateau.
funFacts: The Great Wall of China is not a single continuous wall, but many walls built by different dynasties over centuries.
The Three Gorges Dam is the largest power station in the world by installed capacity.
China has one official time zone for the entire country, despite spanning a width that would normally cover five.
China had the world's largest population for most of recorded history, until India surpassed it in 2023.
The Forbidden City in Beijing served as the imperial palace for 24 emperors across the Ming and Qing dynasties.
Paper, printing, gunpowder and the compass, known as China's 'Four Great Inventions', all originated there.
The Terracotta Army, discovered in 1974, guards the tomb of China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang.
China operates the largest high-speed rail network in the world, spanning tens of thousands of kilometers.
Chinese New Year, based on the lunar calendar, is marked by the world's largest annual human migration as people travel home.
Table tennis is often considered China's unofficial national sport, and the country dominates Olympic competition in it.
cn.territorialNote: China is involved in territorial disputes in the South China Sea with several Southeast Asian neighbors and along its Himalayan border with India, and regards Taiwan as part of its territory, a status Taiwan disputes.

fr.earliestSettlement: Paris began as a Celtic settlement called Lutetia, later developed by the Romans.

keyDates.event: Vercingetorix defeated by Caesar at Alesia, Gaul becomes Roman
Clovis I unites the Franks, founding the Merovingian dynasty
Charlemagne crowned Emperor, founding the Carolingian Empire
Treaty of Verdun creates West Francia, forerunner of France
Hundred Years' War against England begins
Louis XIV's reign begins, the peak of absolute monarchy
French Revolution begins
Napoleon crowned Emperor
Napoleon defeated at Waterloo
Franco-Prussian War leads to the Third Republic
World War I begins
Nazi Germany occupies France
Liberation of Paris from Nazi occupation
Fifth Republic established
Algeria gains independence from France

fr.climate: Mostly temperate oceanic; Mediterranean in the south.
funFacts: France is the world's most-visited country by international tourist arrivals.
The Eiffel Tower was meant to be a temporary structure for the 1889 World's Fair.
France has more time zones than any other country (12), owing to its overseas territories.
The Lumière brothers held what is considered the first public film screening in Paris in 1895, making France a birthplace of cinema.
The Louvre in Paris, home to the Mona Lisa, is the most-visited art museum in the world.
The metric system was developed in France during the French Revolution and has since become the world's dominant system of measurement.
The Tour de France, first held in 1903, is the world's most famous and prestigious cycling race.
French gastronomy was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2010.
The Palace of Versailles, built for Louis XIV, became the model that inspired royal palaces across Europe.
fr.territorialNote: France administers Mayotte as an overseas department, though Comoros claims the island as part of its territory, a dispute dating to Mayotte's 1974 vote to remain with France.

de.earliestSettlement: Germanic tribes inhabited the region from antiquity; Trier, founded by the Romans around 16 BC, claims to be Germany's oldest city.

keyDates.event: Germanic tribes defeat Rome at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
Charlemagne crowned Holy Roman Emperor
Otto I crowned, founding the Holy Roman Empire
Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses spark the Reformation
Thirty Years' War begins, devastating Central Europe
Holy Roman Empire dissolved under Napoleonic pressure
German Empire unified under Prussia
World War I begins
Weimar Republic established
Nazi Party seizes power
Invasion of Poland starts World War II
End of WWII; Germany divided
Berlin Wall built
Fall of the Berlin Wall
German reunification

de.climate: Temperate seasonal, with warm summers and cold (but not extreme) winters.
funFacts: Germany has over 1,500 different types of sausage (Wurst).
The Autobahn is famous for having stretches with no general speed limit.
Germany is home to more than 20,000 castles.
Johannes Gutenberg invented the movable-type printing press in Mainz, Germany, in the mid-15th century, transforming the spread of information.
Munich's Oktoberfest, held every autumn, is the world's largest beer festival and folk festival, drawing millions of visitors.
Karl Benz, working in Mannheim, patented the first true automobile in 1886.
The Berlin Wall divided the city for 28 years, from 1961 until it fell in 1989.
Germany has won the men's FIFA World Cup four times, most recently in 2014.
Germany has over 300 varieties of bread, and bread culture was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2014.
The tradition of decorating Christmas trees is widely believed to have originated in Germany.
de.currencyNote: Germany experienced one of history's most severe hyperinflations in 1923, when the mark's value collapsed and banknotes were issued in denominations of trillions.

jp.earliestSettlement: The Jōmon period, one of the earliest known pottery-making cultures, dates back over 14,000 years in Japan.

keyDates.event: Traditional date of Japan's founding by legendary Emperor Jimmu
Buddhism introduced to Japan from the Korean kingdom of Baekje
Nara established as the first permanent capital
Heian-kyo (Kyoto) becomes the capital, start of the Heian period
Minamoto Yoritomo establishes the Kamakura Shogunate, Japan's first feudal military government
Mongol invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281 are repelled, aided by typhoons ('kamikaze')
Onin War begins, ushering in the Sengoku ('Warring States') period
Portuguese traders and Jesuit missionaries arrive, introducing firearms and Christianity
Tokugawa Shogunate begins, over 250 years of relative isolation
Commodore Perry's 'Black Ships' force Japan to open to foreign trade
Meiji Restoration; Japan rapidly modernizes
First Sino-Japanese War begins
Russo-Japanese War begins
Second Sino-Japanese War begins
WWII ends after atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
New postwar constitution takes effect, renouncing war
Tokyo hosts the first Olympics in Asia
Great East Japan earthquake and tsunami trigger the Fukushima nuclear disaster

jp.climate: Varies north to south: humid continental in Hokkaido to subtropical in Okinawa.
funFacts: Japan's Shinkansen (bullet train) began service in 1964 and has carried billions of passengers with no passenger fatalities from derailment or collision.
Japan has the world's oldest continuously operating company, Kongō Gumi, founded in 578 AD.
Japan consists of over 6,800 islands.
Japan has the world's third-largest economy by nominal GDP.
Sumo wrestling, Japan's national sport, has roots stretching back over a thousand years and retains strict traditional rituals.
Japan sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire and is one of the most seismically active countries on Earth, driving advanced earthquake-resistant building technology.
Japan has one of the highest numbers of centenarians per capita of any country, and life expectancy is among the highest in the world.
Origami, the art of paper folding, originated in Japan and has become an internationally recognized craft.
Mount Fuji and the historic temples and shrines of Kyoto are among Japan's many UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
Vending machines are extraordinarily common across Japan, selling everything from drinks and snacks to hot meals.
Japan is one of the world's largest producers of manga and anime, a major cultural export.
jp.territorialNote: Japan has unresolved territorial disputes, including over the Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands (also claimed by China and Taiwan) and Takeshima/Dokdo (also claimed by South Korea).

in.earliestSettlement: The Indus Valley Civilization, one of the world's earliest urban cultures, flourished from around 3300 BC.

keyDates.event: Indus Valley Civilization at its peak
Ashoka begins his reign, bringing the Maurya Empire to its height
Gupta Empire founded, ushering in a classical golden age
Delhi Sultanate established after the defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan
Mughal Empire founded
British East India Company founded
Battle of Plassey begins British East India Company dominance
British Crown rule begins
Jallianwala Bagh massacre galvanizes the independence movement
Gandhi leads the Salt March against British rule
Independence and Partition, August 15
India becomes a republic
Economic liberalization reforms open up the economy

in.climate: Monsoon-dominated, ranging from tropical in the south to alpine in the Himalayas.
funFacts: India is home to the Statue of Unity, the tallest statue in the world at 182 metres.
India has 22 officially recognized languages and hundreds more spoken regionally.
The game of chess is believed to have originated in India.
India became the world's most populous country, overtaking China, in 2023.
The Taj Mahal, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Agra, was built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a mausoleum for his wife.
India's film industry, centered in Mumbai and often called 'Bollywood,' produces more films annually than any other country.
Yoga, a practice with roots in ancient India, is now practiced by millions worldwide, and June 21 is marked as International Yoga Day.
India is home to a large share of the Himalayas, including some of the world's highest mountains.
The concept of zero as a number was developed in ancient India, revolutionizing mathematics.
India is made up of 28 states and 8 union territories, each with its own languages and cultural traditions.
in.territorialNote: The Kashmir region is divided and claimed in full by both India and Pakistan, and is administered in parts by India, Pakistan, and China.

government.form: Federal elective monarchy (federation of seven emirates)

ae.earliestSettlement: Archaeological sites near Al Ain show settlement dating back over 5,000 years.

keyDates.event: General Maritime Treaty with Britain gives rise to the term 'Trucial States'
Perpetual Maritime Truce signed with Britain
Exclusive Agreements place the Trucial States under British protection
Oil discovered in Abu Dhabi
Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan becomes ruler of Abu Dhabi, driving modernization
United Arab Emirates formed, December 2
Ras Al Khaimah joins the federation as the seventh emirate
UAE dirham introduced as common currency
Emirates airline founded
Sheikh Zayed dies after nearly four decades as president, succeeded by Sheikh Khalifa
Burj Khalifa opens as the world's tallest building

historicalFigures.name: Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan

ae.climate: Arid desert - very hot summers, mild winters.
funFacts: The Burj Khalifa in Dubai is the tallest structure in the world, standing at 828 metres.
The UAE is a federation of seven emirates: Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain, Fujairah, and Ras Al Khaimah.
Dubai International Airport is one of the busiest airports in the world for international passenger traffic.
The Palm Jumeirah is one of the largest artificial islands in the world, visible from space.
The UAE was formed in 1971 when six emirates united, with Ras Al Khaimah joining the federation in 1972.
The UAE's currency, the dirham, has been pegged to the US dollar since 1997.
The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque in Abu Dhabi can hold over 40,000 worshippers and houses one of the world's largest hand-knotted carpets.
Dubai built an indoor ski slope, Ski Dubai, despite average summer temperatures that regularly top 40°C.
In 2020 the UAE launched the Hope Probe, the Arab world's first interplanetary mission, which reached Mars orbit in 2021.
Camel racing, a historic Emirati tradition, now largely uses lightweight robot jockeys following reforms in the 2000s.
Falconry is a deeply rooted Emirati tradition recognized by UNESCO as part of the UAE's intangible cultural heritage.
The UAE hosted the World Expo in Dubai, delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic and held from October 2021 to March 2022.
ae.territorialNote: The UAE disputes Iran's control of Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunb islands in the Persian Gulf.

independence.from: Proclaimed as a republic following the collapse of the Ottoman Empire

tr.earliestSettlement: Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey, dated to around 9500 BC, is among the oldest known temple complexes in the world.

keyDates.event: Hittite Empire rises in central Anatolia, one of the great Bronze Age powers (approx.)
Traditional date for the fall of Troy and the Trojan War (approx.)
Greek city-states begin colonizing the Anatolian (Ionian) coast (approx.)
Constantinople founded as capital of the Roman/Byzantine Empire
Seljuk Turks defeat the Byzantines at the Battle of Manzikert, opening Anatolia to Turkic settlement
Osman I founds the Ottoman beylik, origin of the Ottoman Empire
Ottomans conquer Constantinople
Reign of Suleiman the Magnificent begins, marking the Ottoman Empire's golden age
Ottoman defeat at the Siege of Vienna marks the start of the empire's long decline
Tanzimat reforms begin, modernizing the Ottoman state
Ottoman Empire enters WWI on the side of the Central Powers
Ottoman authorities begin the mass deportation and killing of Armenians
Turkish War of Independence begins under Mustafa Kemal (Atatürk)
Ottoman Sultanate abolished
Republic of Turkey proclaimed, October 29
Mustafa Kemal Atatürk dies
Turkey joins NATO
Major earthquakes in southern Turkey kill tens of thousands

tr.climate: Mediterranean on the coasts, continental in the interior.
funFacts: Istanbul is the only major city in the world that spans two continents, Europe and Asia.
Göbekli Tepe predates Stonehenge by roughly 6,000 years.
Turkey is home to Cappadocia's famous 'fairy chimney' rock formations, shaped by volcanic ash erosion.
Mount Ararat, Turkey's highest peak, is the legendary resting place of Noah's Ark in biblical tradition.
The Hagia Sophia, built in the 6th century as a cathedral, later became a mosque, then a museum, and was reconverted into a mosque in 2020.
Turkish coffee preparation is recognized by UNESCO as part of the world's Intangible Cultural Heritage.
About 3% of Turkey's territory lies in Europe (Thrace), with the rest in Asia (Anatolia), making it one of the world's few transcontinental countries.

funFacts: Canada has the longest coastline of any country in the world.
Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world's lakes combined.
The world's first IMAX film was shown in Canada in 1970.
Canada is the second-largest country in the world by land area, after Russia.
Canada has two official languages, English and French.
Basketball was invented in 1891 by Canadian physical education teacher James Naismith.
The beaver is Canada's national animal and appears on the country's five-cent coin.
Niagara Falls, shared with the United States, is one of the most powerful waterfalls in North America by water flow.
Canada shares the longest land border in the world with a single country, the United States.
Canada produces most of the world's maple syrup, with the majority coming from Quebec.
Ice hockey is widely considered Canada's national winter sport.

funFacts: Australia is the only country that is also a continent.
Over 80% of Australia's plants, mammals, reptiles and frogs are found nowhere else on Earth.
Australia has more venomous snake species than any other country.
The Great Barrier Reef off Australia's northeast coast is the largest living structure on Earth, visible from space.
Aboriginal Australian cultures are among the oldest continuous living cultures in the world, with roots going back at least 65,000 years.
Uluru, a massive sandstone monolith in the Northern Territory, is sacred to the local Anangu people.
Australia was among the first countries in the world to grant women the right to vote and stand in national elections, in 1902.
Australia has no native land predator larger than the dingo, which was introduced by seafarers thousands of years ago.

The Amazon River discharges more water than the next seven largest rivers combined.
Brasilia was purpose-built as the capital and completed in just 41 months.
Brazil is the fifth-largest country in the world by both land area and population.
Rio de Janeiro's Carnival is one of the largest festivals in the world, drawing millions of visitors each year.
Brazil has won the FIFA World Cup a record five times.

Muhammadu Buhari wins election, first opposition candidate to defeat an incumbent president

ng.climate: Tropical, varying from equatorial in the south to semi-arid/Sahel in the far north.
ng.nationalAnimal: Eagle (featured on the coat of arms)
funFacts: Nigeria is Africa's most populous country.
Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, is one of the largest film producers in the world by volume.
Nigeria has over 500 languages spoken within its borders.
Nigeria is Africa's largest economy by GDP.
Afrobeat, a music genre blending jazz, funk, and traditional Yoruba rhythms, was pioneered in Nigeria by Fela Kuti.
Nigeria has won the FIFA U-17 World Cup a record five times.
Zuma Rock, a massive monolith near Abuja, is a well-known natural landmark often called the 'Gateway to Abuja.'
Nigeria is home to over 250 ethnic groups, with Hausa, Yoruba, and Igbo being the largest.
Nigerian writers Wole Soyinka and Chinua Achebe are among Africa's most celebrated literary figures, with Soyinka the first African Nobel laureate in Literature.

pk.independence: August 14, 1947, from the United Kingdom (partition of British India)
pk.earliestSettlement: Home to the Indus Valley Civilization (Mohenjo-daro, c. 2500 BC), one of the world's earliest urban civilizations.

keyDates.event: Indus Valley Civilization flourishes (Mohenjo-daro)
Alexander the Great invades the Indus Valley region
Umayyad general Muhammad bin Qasim conquers Sindh, introducing Islam to the region
Babur founds the Mughal Empire after the Battle of Panipat
Indian Rebellion against British East India Company rule
Partition of India creates Pakistan
First constitution adopted, Islamic Republic declared
First of several military coups (Ayub Khan)
East Pakistan secedes to become Bangladesh
General Zia-ul-Haq seizes power in a military coup
Benazir Bhutto becomes first female prime minister of a Muslim-majority nation
Pakistan conducts nuclear tests
General Pervez Musharraf seizes power in a coup
Return to civilian rule after Musharraf's resignation

pk.climate: Mostly arid/semi-arid, alpine in the mountainous north.
pk.nationalSport: Field hockey (official); cricket is the most popular
funFacts: Pakistan is home to K2, the world's second-highest mountain and one of the most dangerous to climb.
The Indus Valley Civilization, centered in modern Pakistan, had advanced urban planning and sanitation systems 4,500 years ago.
Pakistan has the second-largest Muslim population of any country, after Indonesia.
Pakistan is home to more than 100 peaks over 7,000 meters, making its northern regions a premier destination for mountaineers.
The ancient city of Mohenjo-daro, part of the Indus Valley Civilization, is one of the best-preserved early urban sites in the world.
Pakistan became an independent nation in 1947 following the partition of British India.
Urdu is Pakistan's national language, while English remains an official language used in government and education.
Pakistan won the Cricket World Cup in 1992 under the captaincy of Imran Khan.
pk.territorialNote: Kashmir is a disputed territory divided between India, Pakistan, and China, with the full region claimed by both India and Pakistan.

government.nationalDay: December 5 (birthday of the late King Bhumibol, observed as National Day)

th.earliestSettlement: The Sukhothai Kingdom (founded 1238) is traditionally regarded as the first Thai kingdom; the Ayutthaya Kingdom followed in 1351.

keyDates.event: Sukhothai Kingdom founded, traditional start of the Thai nation
Ayutthaya Kingdom founded
Ayutthaya sacked by Burmese forces, kingdom collapses
King Taksin reunifies the kingdom, founds Thonburi as his capital
Rattanakosin era begins, Bangkok founded as capital
Bowring Treaty opens Siam to free trade with Britain
King Chulalongkorn (Rama V) begins modernizing reforms that help Siam avoid colonization
Revolution ends absolute monarchy, constitutional monarchy begins
Country renamed from Siam to Thailand
Japan invades; Thailand allies with Japan during WWII
Student-led uprising topples the military government
Thammasat University massacre
"Black May" pro-democracy protests force the military government to resign
Asian financial crisis begins with the collapse of the Thai baht
Military coup ousts Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra
King Bhumibol Adulyadej dies after a 70-year reign

th.climate: Tropical, hot and humid with a monsoon season.
funFacts: Thailand is the only Southeast Asian country never colonized by a European power.
Bangkok's full ceremonial name is one of the longest place names in the world.
Thailand is the world's largest exporter of canned tuna.
Thailand is also the world's largest exporter of natural rubber.
Muay Thai, Thai boxing, is the national sport and a martial art now practiced and competed in worldwide.
Thailand has more than 1,400 islands, with Phuket and the Phi Phi Islands among its most famous tourist destinations.
Thailand's New Year festival, Songkran, is celebrated each April with a nationwide water fight.
Thailand is home to the Kitti's hog-nosed bat, found in limestone caves and often regarded as one of the world's smallest mammals.
The Grand Palace and Wat Arun in Bangkok are among Southeast Asia's most visited royal and religious landmarks.

vn.independence: September 2, 1945 (declared from France/Japan); formally recognized after the First Indochina War, 1954
formerNames: Democratic Republic of Vietnam / Republic of Vietnam (divided 1954-1975)
vn.earliestSettlement: Vietnamese civilization traces back to the Hong Bang dynasty (traditionally from c. 2879 BC) and the Dong Son culture of the Bronze Age.

keyDates.event: Beginning of roughly 1,000 years of Chinese rule
Ngo Quyen defeats Chinese forces at the Bach Dang River, ending Chinese rule
Ly dynasty moves the capital to Thang Long (modern Hanoi)
Tran dynasty repels a Mongol invasion at the Bach Dang River
Le Loi founds the Le dynasty after expelling Ming Chinese occupiers
Nguyen dynasty unifies Vietnam under Emperor Gia Long
France begins its conquest of Vietnam
French Indochina established
Ho Chi Minh declares independence
Battle of Dien Bien Phu ends French rule; country divided at 17th parallel
US combat troops arrive, escalating the Vietnam War
Fall of Saigon, Vietnam War ends, country reunified
Doi Moi economic reforms begin
Vietnam normalizes diplomatic relations with the United States

vn.climate: Tropical in the south, monsoonal with a more temperate winter in the north.
vn.nationalSport: Vo vietnam (martial art); football is the most popular spectator sport
funFacts: Vietnam is the world's second-largest coffee exporter after Brazil.
The Vietnam War is known domestically as the 'American War.'
Ha Long Bay contains around 1,600 limestone islands and islets.
Vietnam is the world's largest exporter of cashew nuts.
The ao dai, a long tunic worn over trousers, is Vietnam's traditional national dress.
Vietnam stretches more than 1,600 km from north to south but is in places less than 50 km wide.
Pho, a noodle soup, is widely considered Vietnam's unofficial national dish.
Vietnam was divided into North and South from 1954 until reunification in 1975.
The Cu Chi tunnels near Ho Chi Minh City are a vast underground network used during the Vietnam War.
Water puppetry, a centuries-old art form performed on a water stage, originated in the Red River Delta of northern Vietnam.

pl.independence: November 11, 1918 (re-established after 123 years of partition between Russia, Prussia and Austria)
pl.earliestSettlement: The Polish state traditionally dates to 966 AD, when Duke Mieszko I converted to Christianity (the Baptism of Poland).

keyDates.event: Baptism of Poland, traditional founding of the Polish state
Boleslaw I Chrobry crowned first King of Poland
Krakow Academy (later Jagiellonian University) founded, among the oldest in Central Europe
Union of Krewo begins the dynastic union of Poland and Lithuania
Battle of Grunwald: Polish-Lithuanian forces defeat the Teutonic Knights
Union of Lublin creates the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
Constitution of 3 May adopted, Europe's first modern codified national constitution
Third Partition erases Poland from the map for 123 years
Poland regains independence
Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union invade, starting WWII
Warsaw Uprising against German occupation is crushed
Soviet-backed communist government installed after WWII
Solidarity trade union founded, led by Lech Walesa
Solidarity movement leads to the fall of communism
Poland joins NATO
Poland joins the European Union

pl.climate: Temperate, transitional between oceanic and continental.
funFacts: Poland disappeared from the map of Europe for 123 years (1795-1918) after being partitioned by its neighbors.
Nicolaus Copernicus, Marie Curie and Frederic Chopin were all Polish.
The Wieliczka Salt Mine has been in continuous operation since the 13th century and includes entire chapels carved from salt.
Poland's Bialowieza Forest is one of the last and largest remaining parts of the primeval forest that once covered the European Plain, home to free-roaming European bison.
The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth's Constitution of 3 May 1791 was the first modern written constitution in Europe and the second in the world after the United States.
Krakow's St. Mary's Basilica features an hourly trumpet signal that stops abruptly mid-note, commemorating a trumpeter struck by an arrow while warning of a Mongol attack.
Poland is one of the largest apple producers in the European Union.
Pierogi, Poland's iconic dumplings, are traditionally eaten on Christmas Eve and come in both sweet and savory varieties.
Torun, birthplace of Copernicus, is also famous for its centuries-old gingerbread (piernik) baking tradition.
Warsaw's Old Town was almost entirely destroyed in World War II and then meticulously rebuilt from historic paintings and photographs, earning it UNESCO World Heritage status.
In 1985, Polish surgeon Zbigniew Religa performed the country's first successful heart transplant.
pl.currencyNote: Poland redenominated its currency in 1995, replacing 10,000 old złoty with 1 new złoty after the hyperinflation of the early 1990s.

nl.independence: Formally recognized 1648 (Peace of Westphalia), following the Union of Utrecht 1579
nl.earliestSettlement: Low-lying delta lands settled since prehistoric times; the Dutch Republic rose to global prominence as a major trading and colonial power in the 17th-century 'Golden Age.'

keyDates.event: Burgundian dukes unify much of the Low Countries
Iconoclastic Fury marks the outbreak of the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule
Union of Utrecht, founding basis of the Dutch Republic
Dutch East India Company founded, world's first multinational corporation
Peace of Westphalia formally recognizes Dutch independence from Spain
First Anglo-Dutch War begins
French Revolutionary forces establish the Batavian Republic
Kingdom of the Netherlands established under William I
Belgium secedes from the Netherlands
Nazi Germany invades and occupies the Netherlands
Hunger Winter famine strikes during the final months of Nazi occupation
Founding member of the European Economic Community
Euro adopted as the national currency

nl.climate: Temperate maritime, mild winters and cool summers.
nl.nationalSport: Football (soccer); speed skating and cycling culturally significant
funFacts: About a third of the Netherlands lies at or below sea level, reclaimed and protected by dikes and pumps.
The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, is considered the world's first publicly traded company.
The Netherlands is the world's second-largest exporter of food by value, despite its small size.
The Netherlands is the world's largest exporter of tulip bulbs and cut flowers.
Amsterdam has more canals and bridges than Venice.
The Dutch are, on average, the tallest people in the world.
Dutch painters Rembrandt and Vermeer produced some of the most celebrated works of the 17th-century 'Dutch Golden Age.'
There are more bicycles than people in the Netherlands, and cycling is central to everyday Dutch life.
The Netherlands became the first country in the world to legalize same-sex marriage, in 2001.
nl.currencyNote: The Netherlands replaced its guilder with the euro in 2002 as part of the eurozone currency union.

gr.independence: Independence declared March 25, 1821, from the Ottoman Empire (recognized 1830)
gr.earliestSettlement: Birthplace of Western civilization; Minoan and Mycenaean civilizations flourished from around 3000-1100 BC, followed by Classical Greece.

keyDates.event: Traditional date of the first Olympic Games
Athenian democracy established under Cleisthenes
Battle of Marathon; Athens repels the first Persian invasion
Alexander the Great becomes king of Macedon and begins his conquests
Constantinople founded as capital of the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire
Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
Fall of Constantinople ends the Byzantine Empire
Greek War of Independence begins
Greek independence formally recognized
Balkan Wars expand Greek territory
Nazi Germany occupies Greece during WWII
Greek Civil War begins (ends 1949)
Military junta seizes power ("Regime of the Colonels")
Democracy restored after the junta collapses
Greece joins the European Economic Community
Greece adopts the euro

gr.climate: Mediterranean, hot dry summers and mild wet winters.
funFacts: Greece is considered the birthplace of democracy, Western philosophy and the Olympic Games.
Greece has more archaeological museums than any other country in the world.
The Greek alphabet is the ancestor of both the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets.
The Parthenon in Athens, built in the 5th century BC, was dedicated to the goddess Athena.
Greece enjoys more annual sunshine hours than almost any other European country, making tourism a pillar of its economy.
The modern Olympic Games were revived in Athens in 1896, inspired by the ancient games held at Olympia.
Greek mythology, with gods such as Zeus, Athena, and Poseidon, has profoundly shaped Western literature and art.
Greece has thousands of islands, though only around 200 of them are inhabited.
Mount Olympus, Greece's highest mountain, was believed by the ancient Greeks to be the home of the gods.
Greek cuisine staples like olive oil, feta cheese, and moussaka are enjoyed around the world today.

ke.earliestSettlement: Among the earliest regions of hominid evolution (fossils found at Lake Turkana date back millions of years); coastal Swahili city-states traded with Arabia and India from around the 1st century AD.

keyDates.event: Swahili city-states such as Mombasa and Lamu flourish as Indian Ocean trade hubs (approx.)
Vasco da Gama reaches the Kenyan coast, opening Portuguese contact
British East Africa Protectorate established
Kenya becomes a British Crown colony
Mau Mau uprising against colonial rule begins
Independence from Britain
Republic of Kenya proclaimed, Jomo Kenyatta first president
President Jomo Kenyatta dies, succeeded by Daniel arap Moi
Mwai Kibaki elected president, ending Moi's 24-year rule
Disputed election sparks nationwide post-election violence
New constitution adopted, devolving power to counties

ke.climate: Varies from tropical along the coast to arid in the north and temperate in the highlands.
ke.nationalSport: Athletics (long-distance running); rugby sevens also notable
funFacts: Kenya has produced a disproportionate number of the world's elite long-distance runners, especially from the Rift Valley region.
Nairobi National Park is one of the only national parks in the world located within a capital city.
Kenya pioneered mobile money with M-Pesa, launched in 2007, now used by most of the adult population.
Mount Kenya, the country's highest peak and Africa's second-highest mountain, gave the country its name.
The Great Rift Valley runs through Kenya and is often called the 'Cradle of Humankind' due to important fossil discoveries of early human ancestors.
The annual Great Migration, in which millions of wildebeest and zebra cross between Kenya's Maasai Mara and Tanzania's Serengeti, is one of the largest wildlife spectacles on Earth.
Kenya gained independence from Britain in 1963 after years of colonial rule.
Swahili and English are both official languages of Kenya.
Kenya is home to more than 40 different ethnic groups, each with distinct languages and traditions.
The Maasai people of Kenya are known for their distinctive red shuka clothing and traditional jumping dance, the adumu.
ke.territorialNote: Kenya and Somalia had a maritime boundary dispute in the Indian Ocean, which was resolved by the International Court of Justice in 2021.

et.independence: Never formally colonized (briefly occupied by Italy 1936-1941); one of the oldest independent nations in the world
et.earliestSettlement: Home to some of the earliest known hominid fossils (including 'Lucy'); the Kingdom of Aksum, founded around the 1st century AD, was a major ancient trading power.

keyDates.event: Kingdom of Aksum rises as a major trading empire
Aksum adopts Christianity under King Ezana
Solomonic dynasty established, claiming descent from Solomon and Sheba
Ethiopian-Adal War begins, led by Ahmad Gragn
Tewodros II begins the modern unification of Ethiopia
Battle of Adwa - Ethiopia defeats Italy, preserving independence
Italian occupation begins (ends 1941)
Liberation from Italy, Emperor Haile Selassie restored
Haile Selassie overthrown, Derg military regime takes power
Derg military regime falls, Eritrea later separates (1993)
Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia established
Abiy Ahmed becomes prime minister, signs peace deal with Eritrea

et.climate: Highly varied by elevation - temperate highlands, hot lowlands including the Danakil Depression, one of the hottest places on Earth.
funFacts: Ethiopia is the only African country never colonized by a European power.
Ethiopia uses its own calendar, which runs roughly seven to eight years behind the Gregorian calendar.
Ethiopia is widely considered the birthplace of coffee, originating in the Kaffa region.
The Ethiopian calendar has 13 months — twelve of 30 days and a short thirteenth month of five or six days.
The 3.2-million-year-old hominid fossil nicknamed 'Lucy', a landmark discovery in human evolution, was found in Ethiopia in 1974.
Ethiopia follows its own time system, in which the day traditionally begins at dawn rather than at midnight.
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia's capital, hosts the headquarters of the African Union and is often called the diplomatic capital of Africa.
Ethiopian runner Abebe Bikila won the 1960 Rome Olympic marathon while running barefoot, becoming the first sub-Saharan African to win an Olympic gold medal.
Ethiopia has long been a powerhouse in distance running, producing numerous Olympic and world champions.
et.territorialNote: The border town of Badme and surrounding areas were disputed between Ethiopia and Eritrea following their 1998-2000 war; an international boundary commission awarded the area to Eritrea in 2002, a ruling Ethiopia formally accepted as part of a 2018 peace agreement.

pe.earliestSettlement: Home to the Norte Chico civilization (one of the oldest in the Americas, c. 3500 BC) and later the Inca Empire, the largest empire in pre-Columbian America.

keyDates.event: Chavin culture, one of the earliest major Andean civilizations, flourishes
Moche civilization flourishes along the northern coast
Kingdom of Chimor rises along the northern coast
Inca Empire begins rapid expansion under Pachacuti
Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro captures the Inca emperor Atahualpa
Pizarro founds Lima as the new colonial capital
Viceroyalty of Peru established, becomes the center of Spanish South America
Tupac Amaru II leads a major indigenous uprising against Spanish rule
Independence declared by Jose de San Martin
Battle of Ayacucho secures final independence from Spain
War of the Pacific against Chile begins, Peru loses territory
Machu Picchu brought to international attention by Hiram Bingham
Military coup brings Juan Velasco Alvarado to power, launches major land reforms
Shining Path insurgency begins (internal conflict through the 1990s-2000s)
President Alberto Fujimori dissolves Congress in a self-coup

pe.climate: Highly varied - arid coastal desert, alpine Andean highlands, tropical Amazon rainforest.
pe.nationalSport: Football (soccer); paleta frontón is the official traditional sport
funFacts: Machu Picchu was unknown to the outside world until 1911 and was never found by the Spanish conquistadors.
The Nazca Lines, giant geoglyphs in the desert, are best seen from the air and were made over 1,500 years ago.
Peru is home to over 4,000 varieties of potato, the plant's center of origin.
Peru is home to Lake Titicaca, the highest navigable lake in the world, shared with Bolivia.
Ceviche, Peru's national dish of fish marinated in citrus, has UNESCO-recognized culinary roots.
Peru was the heartland of the Inca Empire, the largest empire in pre-Columbian America.
Some of the most remote headwaters of the Amazon River rise in the Peruvian Andes.
Peru contains three strikingly different geographic regions - a coastal desert, the Andean highlands, and Amazon rainforest - within a relatively compact territory.
pe.currencyNote: Peru suffered severe hyperinflation in the late 1980s, leading to the replacement of the inti with the new sol in 1991.

co.independence: July 20, 1810 (declared); fully secured 1819 after the Battle of Boyaca, from Spain
formerNames: Gran Colombia (1819-1831, including Venezuela, Ecuador, Panama)
co.earliestSettlement: Home to pre-Columbian cultures including the Muisca, known for the legend of El Dorado; Spanish founded Santa Marta in 1525, one of South America's oldest cities.

keyDates.event: Muisca Confederation flourishes in the central highlands, a goldworking culture behind the El Dorado legend
Spanish found Santa Marta
Gonzalo Jimenez de Quesada founds Santa Fe de Bogota
Viceroyalty of New Granada established
Declaration of independence from Spain
Simon Bolivar wins independence at the Battle of Boyaca
Gran Colombia dissolves into separate republics
Thousand Days War civil war begins
Panama separates from Colombia (with US backing)
Assassination of Jorge Eliecer Gaitan sparks the Bogotazo and a decade of La Violencia
FARC guerrilla group founded
Peace accord signed with FARC guerrillas, ending decades of conflict

co.climate: Tropical along the coasts and Amazon, temperate in the Andean highlands.
co.nationalSport: Tejo (official); football is the most popular
funFacts: Colombia is the world's second most biodiverse country, after Brazil, despite being far smaller.
The legend of El Dorado originated from a Muisca ritual near Bogota involving gold dust and a sacred lake.
Colombia is the only South American country with coastlines on both the Pacific and Atlantic (Caribbean).
Colombia is the world's leading producer of emeralds.
Coffee growing is central to Colombian culture and the country remains one of the world's largest coffee exporters.
The Colombian Andes split into three parallel mountain ranges, or cordilleras, as they cross the country.
Cartagena's walled colonial old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its Spanish colonial architecture.
Colombia is home to more recorded bird species than any other country in the world.

ph.independence: June 12, 1898, from Spain (declared); full sovereignty from the United States recognized July 4, 1946
ph.earliestSettlement: Inhabited by diverse ethnic groups for thousands of years; Ferdinand Magellan's expedition reached the islands in 1521, beginning Spanish contact.

keyDates.event: Laguna Copperplate Inscription, the earliest known written document in Philippine history
Islam introduced in the southern Philippines by Arab and Malay traders
Magellan's expedition arrives, first European contact
Spanish colonization formally begins under Miguel Lopez de Legazpi
Manila founded as the Spanish colonial capital
Philippine Revolution against Spain begins, led by Andres Bonifacio
Philippine independence declared by Emilio Aguinaldo
Spanish-American War ends; Philippines ceded to the US
Philippine-American War begins following US annexation
Commonwealth of the Philippines established under US tutelage
Japanese occupation begins during WWII
Full independence from the United States granted
Ferdinand Marcos elected president
Marcos declares martial law
People Power Revolution ousts Ferdinand Marcos
Mount Pinatubo erupts, one of the largest volcanic eruptions of the 20th century

ph.climate: Tropical maritime, hot and humid with a distinct typhoon season.
ph.nationalSport: Arnis/Eskrima (official); basketball is overwhelmingly the most popular

unesco.name: Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras

funFacts: The Philippines consists of over 7,600 islands.
The Philippines was named after King Philip II of Spain.
Filipino text messaging habits once made the Philippines the 'texting capital of the world.'
The Philippines was a Spanish colony for over 300 years before becoming a US territory in 1898, finally gaining full independence in 1946.
Jeepneys, colorful repurposed military jeeps, became an iconic form of public transport in the Philippines after World War II.
The Philippines is one of the largest predominantly Christian nations in Asia, a legacy of Spanish colonization.
Boracay and Palawan are frequently ranked among the best beach destinations in the world.
The 1986 'People Power Revolution' was a largely peaceful uprising that ousted President Ferdinand Marcos.

my.independence: August 31, 1957 (Malaya, from the United Kingdom); Malaysia formed September 16, 1963 with Sabah, Sarawak and (briefly) Singapore
my.earliestSettlement: The Malacca Sultanate, founded around 1400, became a major trading hub connecting East and West along the Strait of Malacca.

keyDates.event: Malacca Sultanate founded, becomes a major trade hub
Portuguese conquer Malacca, beginning European colonial presence
British East India Company establishes a settlement on Penang Island
Straits Settlements formed (Penang, Malacca, Singapore)
Federated Malay States formed under British control
Japanese occupation of Malaya begins during WWII
Malayan Emergency begins, a communist insurgency lasting until 1960
Independence of Malaya from Britain
Formation of Malaysia (Malaya, Sabah, Sarawak, Singapore)
Singapore separates from Malaysia
May 13 racial riots lead to major policy changes, including the New Economic Policy

my.climate: Tropical rainforest, hot and humid year-round.

unesco.name: Historic Cities of the Straits of Malacca

funFacts: The Petronas Towers were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004.
Malaysia is split between Peninsular Malaysia and East Malaysia (on the island of Borneo), separated by the South China Sea.
Malaysia is one of the most linguistically and ethnically diverse countries in Southeast Asia.
Malaysia is one of the world's leading producers of palm oil, a major export crop.
The rainforests of Malaysian Borneo are among the oldest in the world, estimated at well over 100 million years old.
Batu Caves, near Kuala Lumpur, houses a Hindu temple complex and one of the tallest statues of the deity Murugan in the world.
Nasi lemak, rice cooked in coconut milk and served with sambal, is widely regarded as Malaysia's national dish.
Malaysia operates a dual legal system, with civil law existing alongside Sharia law applied to Muslim citizens in certain matters.
Malaysia built its own national car industry, Proton, making it one of the few Southeast Asian countries to do so.

sg.independence: August 9, 1965, separation from Malaysia (fully self-governing from Britain in 1959)
sg.earliestSettlement: A trading settlement existed as early as the 14th century; modern Singapore was founded as a British trading post by Sir Stamford Raffles in 1819.

keyDates.event: Traditional founding of the Kingdom of Singapura
Stamford Raffles establishes a British trading post
Singapore joins the Straits Settlements with Penang and Malacca
Straits Settlements become a British Crown Colony
Japanese occupation begins during WWII (ends 1945)
Singapore achieves self-governance; Lee Kuan Yew becomes Prime Minister
Joins the Federation of Malaysia
Separates from Malaysia, becomes fully independent
Lee Kuan Yew steps down after 31 years as Prime Minister
Lee Kuan Yew dies

sg.climate: Tropical rainforest, hot and humid year-round with no distinct seasons.
naturalResources: Minimal natural resources; relies on trade, finance and services
sg.nationalAnimal: Lion (symbolic - Merlion); the Singapore name derives from Sanskrit 'Lion City'
funFacts: Singapore transformed from a small trading port into one of the world's wealthiest nations in roughly two generations.
Chewing gum sale has been restricted in Singapore since 1992.
Singapore's name comes from the Sanskrit 'Singapura,' meaning 'Lion City.'
Singapore is one of only three city-states in the modern world, alongside Monaco and Vatican City.
Changi Airport's Jewel complex features the world's tallest indoor waterfall alongside a rooftop swimming pool and butterfly garden found elsewhere on the airport grounds.
Singapore has one of the busiest container ports in the world, a key hub for global shipping trade.
Hawker centers in Singapore, open-air food courts, were added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2020.
Singapore has four official languages: English, Malay, Mandarin Chinese and Tamil.
Gardens by the Bay's futuristic 'Supertrees' are vertical gardens up to 50 meters tall that also function as solar collectors.

nz.independence: September 26, 1907 (Dominion status); full legislative independence via the Statute of Westminster, adopted 1947
nz.earliestSettlement: Settled by Polynesian voyagers (ancestors of the Maori) around 1250-1300 AD, one of the last major landmasses to be settled by humans.

keyDates.event: Maori settlement of New Zealand begins (approx.)
Abel Tasman becomes the first European to sight New Zealand
James Cook charts New Zealand's coastline
Treaty of Waitangi signed between the British Crown and Maori chiefs
New Zealand Wars begin between Maori and colonial forces
New Zealand becomes the first self-governing country to grant women the vote
Becomes a Dominion within the British Empire
Adopts the Statute of Westminster, gaining full legislative independence
Declares itself nuclear-free
Major earthquake devastates Christchurch

nz.climate: Temperate maritime, mild with no extreme seasonal temperatures.
funFacts: New Zealand was the first country in the world to grant women the right to vote, in 1893.
New Zealand has more sheep than people, though the ratio has shrunk significantly in recent decades.
The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit film trilogies were shot almost entirely in New Zealand.
New Zealand has no native land mammals apart from two species of bat, which let unique birds like the kiwi and kakapo evolve without ground predators.
New Zealand was among the first countries to officially adopt the eight-hour working day, in the 19th century.
Rugby union is New Zealand's national sport, and the All Blacks perform the haka, a traditional Maori challenge, before matches.
New Zealand's currency, the New Zealand dollar, is commonly nicknamed the 'Kiwi.'
Because of its position near the International Date Line, New Zealand is among the first places on Earth to greet each new day.

is.independence: June 17, 1944, from Denmark (full republic established; home rule had existed since 1918)
is.earliestSettlement: Settled by Norse and Celtic peoples beginning around 874 AD, traditionally led by Ingolfur Arnarson, who founded Reykjavik.

keyDates.event: Traditional date of Norse settlement, Ingolfur Arnarson founds Reykjavik
Althing established - one of the world's oldest parliaments
Iceland adopts Christianity by law at the Althing
Iceland submits to Norwegian rule
Iceland comes under the Kalmar Union, later sole Danish rule
Lutheran Reformation completed with the execution of the last Catholic bishop
Laki volcanic eruption causes famine that kills roughly a fifth of Iceland's population
Denmark grants Iceland its first constitution and home rule
Act of Union grants Iceland sovereignty under the Danish crown
Republic of Iceland founded, full independence from Denmark
Vigdís Finnbogadóttir becomes the world's first democratically elected female president
Icelandic banking system collapses in a major financial crisis

is.climate: Subarctic/tundra, moderated by the Gulf Stream; cool summers, mild (for the latitude) winters.
funFacts: Iceland's Althing, founded in 930 AD, is considered one of the oldest surviving parliaments in the world.
Iceland has no standing army and runs almost entirely on renewable geothermal and hydro energy.
Iceland is one of the most volcanically active places on Earth, sitting on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Iceland has no mosquitoes, one of the only places in the world where they cannot survive.
The Icelandic sagas, written down in the 13th century, are among the great works of medieval literature and record the Viking settlement of the island.
Iceland was the first country in the world to democratically elect a female head of state, Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, in 1980.
The Blue Lagoon geothermal spa formed by accident, fed by the warm outflow of a nearby geothermal power plant.
Iceland sits on the boundary between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates, which are slowly pulling apart.
Reykjavik is the northernmost capital city of any sovereign state in the world.
Icelanders traditionally use patronymic surnames, so phone directories are commonly sorted by first name rather than surname.

ie.climate: Temperate maritime, mild and changeable with frequent rainfall.
funFacts: Newgrange in Ireland predates both Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza.
Ireland's low corporate tax rate has made it the European base for many major US tech and pharmaceutical companies.
The Irish diaspora is enormous - tens of millions of people worldwide claim Irish ancestry, far outnumbering Ireland's own population.
Guinness, the famous stout, has been brewed at Dublin's St. James's Gate since 1759.
Ireland is nicknamed the 'Emerald Isle' for its lush green countryside, a result of its mild, rainy climate.
St. Patrick's Day, honoring Ireland's patron saint, is celebrated with parades around the world, far beyond Ireland itself.
Ireland has produced four Nobel laureates in Literature: W.B. Yeats, George Bernard Shaw, Samuel Beckett, and Seamus Heaney.
Traditional Irish music, featuring instruments like the fiddle, tin whistle, and bodhran, remains a living tradition in pubs across the country.
The Cliffs of Moher, rising up to 214 meters above the Atlantic, are one of Ireland's most visited natural attractions.

se.nationalSport: Football (soccer); ice hockey also hugely popular
funFacts: Sweden has not fought a war since 1814, one of the longest periods of sustained peace of any nation.
The Nobel Prizes are awarded in Stockholm (except the Peace Prize, awarded in Oslo), funded by Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel's estate.
Sweden pioneered the modern concept of 'fika,' a dedicated coffee-and-cake social break woven into daily work life.
Sweden is the birthplace of IKEA, Spotify and the pop group ABBA, making it one of Europe's most influential exporters of design, music and technology.
The Swedish concept of 'allemansratten' (the right to roam) allows anyone to walk, cycle or camp on most land, public or private, as long as they respect nature and privacy.
Sweden has more than 95,000 lakes and thousands of islands, including the Stockholm archipelago with around 30,000 islands and skerries.
The Vasa Museum in Stockholm houses a nearly fully intact 17th-century warship that sank on its maiden voyage in 1628 and was raised from the seabed in 1961.
Sweden was among the first countries to introduce paid parental leave that can be shared between both parents.
Midsummer is one of Sweden's most important holidays, traditionally celebrated with dancing around a flower-decked maypole.

no.earliestSettlement: Settled since the end of the last ice age; the Viking Age (c. 793-1066) saw Norwegian seafarers explore and settle as far as Iceland, Greenland and briefly North America.

no.nationalAnimal: Lion (on the coat of arms, though not native)

unesco.name: West Norwegian Fjords - Geirangerfjord and Naeroyfjord

funFacts: Norway's sovereign wealth fund, built on oil revenue, is the largest in the world.
Norway has the world's longest road tunnel, the Laerdal Tunnel, at over 24 km.
Parts of northern Norway experience the midnight sun in summer and polar night in winter.
Norway was the birthplace of modern competitive skiing, and the sport remains central to its national identity.
The Norwegian fjords, carved by glaciers, include Geirangerfjord and Naeroyfjord, both UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
Norway was united with Denmark and later Sweden for centuries before gaining full independence in 1905.
The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo, while the other Nobel Prizes are awarded in Sweden.
Norway consistently ranks among the happiest and most developed countries in international indices.

unesco.name: Jelling Mounds, Runic Stones and Church

funFacts: The Danish monarchy is one of the oldest continuous monarchies in the world, tracing back over 1,000 years.
Lego, the world-famous toy brick, was invented in Denmark in 1932.
Denmark consistently ranks among the world's happiest countries.
The Dannebrog, Denmark's flag, is traditionally regarded as the oldest continuously used national flag still in use today.
Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales, including 'The Little Mermaid' and 'The Ugly Duckling', were written in Denmark and are known worldwide.
Copenhagen is consistently ranked among the most bicycle-friendly cities in the world, with more bikes than cars in the city centre.
Greenland and the Faroe Islands are autonomous territories within the Kingdom of Denmark.
Denmark generates a substantial share of its electricity from wind power and was an early pioneer of wind turbine technology.
The Jelling Stones, raised in the 10th century, are considered Denmark's 'birth certificate' as a unified, Christian nation.

fi.earliestSettlement: Inhabited since the end of the last ice age; came under Swedish rule from the 12th century, then ceded to Russia in 1809 as an autonomous Grand Duchy.

funFacts: Finland has been ranked the world's happiest country for multiple consecutive years in the World Happiness Report.
Finland has more saunas than cars, with an estimated 2-3 million saunas for a population of around 5.5 million.
Nokia, now famous for phones, started in 1865 as a wood pulp mill.
Finland has more than 180,000 lakes, earning it the nickname 'Land of a Thousand Lakes'.
In 1906, Finland became the first country in the world to grant women full political rights, including the right to stand for election.
Finland's Lapland region is marketed as the official home of Santa Claus, centred on the city of Rovaniemi.
Finland joined NATO in 2023, ending decades of military non-alignment, after sharing a long border with Russia.
Finnish children typically start formal schooling at age seven, and the country's education system is consistently ranked among the world's best.
The town of Sonkajärvi hosts the annual Wife Carrying World Championships.

ch.earliestSettlement: Alpine region inhabited since prehistoric times; the modern confederation traces its founding to the Rutli Oath of 1291 among three forest cantons.

Switzerland is not a member of the European Union, though it participates in the Schengen passport-free travel area.
CERN, home to the Large Hadron Collider, straddles the Swiss-French border near Geneva.
Switzerland is a confederation of 26 cantons, each with significant local autonomy.
Swiss citizens vote in national referendums more often than almost any other country, a hallmark of its direct democracy.
Switzerland is closely associated with the invention of milk chocolate and remains one of the world's top chocolate producers.
The Swiss Alps cover roughly 60% of the country's total land area.
Switzerland has no official capital city; Bern is the de facto seat of government, chosen in 1848 as a compromise among the cantons.

at.independence: Modern republic re-established 1955 (State Treaty, ending post-WWII Allied occupation); Austria existed as a state for centuries before
at.earliestSettlement: Vienna's site was settled since Celtic and Roman times (Roman camp Vindobona); the Babenberg dynasty established Austria as a distinct march in 976 AD.

The Vienna State Opera and Vienna Philharmonic have made the city one of the world's great centers of classical music.
Austria's highest peak, the Grossglockner, is crossed by the Grossglockner High Alpine Road, a famous scenic mountain route.
Sigmund Freud, the founder of psychoanalysis, lived and worked in Vienna for most of his career.
Austria was annexed by Nazi Germany in the 1938 Anschluss and remained under Allied occupation until 1955.
Though filmed largely in the United States, The Sound of Music is set in and around Salzburg, Austria.
The Swarovski crystal company, founded in Austria in 1895, remains one of the world's best-known makers of cut crystal glassware.

The comic character Tintin, created by Belgian artist Hergé, has been translated into more than 100 languages.

Lisbon's Livraria Bertrand, founded in 1732, is recognized as the oldest bookstore still in operation in the world.
Fado, a melancholic traditional music genre, is recognized by UNESCO as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
The Vasco da Gama Bridge in Lisbon is the longest bridge in Europe.
Port wine, named after the city of Porto, can only carry that name if it comes from the Douro Valley region.
The devastating 1755 Lisbon earthquake helped give rise to the modern scientific study of seismology.
Portugal enjoys more hours of sunshine per year than almost any other country in Europe.
Cristiano Ronaldo, one of the most famous footballers in history, was born on the Portuguese island of Madeira.

Paprika, made from ground peppers, is a defining spice in Hungarian cuisine, especially in dishes like goulash.

Gregor Mendel, the 'father of modern genetics', carried out his pioneering pea-plant experiments at a monastery in Brno.
Franz Kafka, one of the most influential writers of the 20th century, was born and lived most of his life in Prague.
The term 'defenestration' entered political vocabulary partly because of two famous incidents in Prague, in 1419 and 1618, where officials were thrown from windows.

Ukraine is the largest country whose territory lies entirely within Europe.
The 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster occurred in northern Ukraine, and the surrounding exclusion zone remains largely uninhabited today.
Borscht, Ukraine's beetroot soup, was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in 2022.

The Carpathian Mountains cross western Ukraine and are home to the highland Hutsul culture.

Pysanky, intricately patterned Easter eggs made with a wax-resist dyeing technique, are a centuries-old Ukrainian folk art.

The Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest is the heaviest building in the world.
The Carpathian Mountains that arc through Romania shelter one of the largest populations of brown bears, wolves and lynx in Europe.
Romania's Painted Monasteries of northern Moldavia feature elaborate exterior frescoes that have survived outdoors for centuries.
Gymnast Nadia Comaneci, competing for Romania at the 1976 Montreal Olympics, was the first gymnast ever awarded a perfect score of 10.
The Danube Delta in Romania is Europe's largest and best-preserved wetland, protected as a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve.

Romania is one of the world's leading producers of plum brandy (tuica), distilled from the country's abundant plum orchards.
