rs.independence: Recognized 1878 (Congress of Berlin, from the Ottoman Empire); modern republic re-established 2006 after the dissolution of Serbia and Montenegro
formerNames: Federal Republic of Yugoslavia / Serbia and Montenegro
rs.earliestSettlement: Serbian medieval statehood traces to the Principality of Serbia in the 8th-9th centuries, with the Nemanjic dynasty (from 1166) building a powerful medieval kingdom and empire.

keyDates.event: Nemanjic dynasty founded, beginning Serbia's medieval golden age
Serbia becomes a kingdom under Stefan the First-Crowned
Stefan Dusan proclaims the Serbian Empire at its medieval height
Battle of Kosovo against the Ottomans, central to Serbian national memory
Ottoman conquest completes, centuries of Ottoman rule follow
First Serbian Uprising against Ottoman rule
Second Serbian Uprising secures autonomy
Independence recognized at the Congress of Berlin
Serbia becomes the core of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
Axis powers invade and occupy Yugoslavia
Communist Yugoslavia established under Tito
NATO bombing campaign over the Kosovo conflict
Serbia becomes fully independent after Montenegro's secession
Kosovo unilaterally declares independence from Serbia

rs.climate: Temperate continental, warm summers, cold winters.
rs.nationalAnimal: Grey wolf; white eagle also a major historic symbol
rs.nationalSport: Football (soccer); basketball and water polo also internationally elite
funFacts: Nikola Tesla, the pioneering inventor and engineer, was born to Serbian parents in what is now Croatia and is a Serbian national icon.
Belgrade is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, with settlement dating back over 7,000 years.
The Belgrade Fortress sits at the confluence of the Sava and Danube rivers, a strategically contested site for millennia.
Novak Djokovic, one of the greatest tennis players in history, was born in Belgrade and holds the record for most Grand Slam men's singles titles.
Serbia is one of the world's largest producers of raspberries.
The EXIT music festival, held annually at the Petrovaradin Fortress in Novi Sad, is one of Europe's best-known summer festivals.
Medieval Serbia's Nemanjic dynasty left behind monasteries such as Studenica, which are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
Landlocked Serbia sits at the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkans, historically a strategic route between Central Europe and the Near East.
rs.territorialNote: Serbia regards Kosovo, which declared independence in 2008 and has been recognized by many but not all UN member states, as part of its sovereign territory.

sk.independence: January 1, 1993 (Slovakia formed from the peaceful dissolution of Czechoslovakia)
formerNames: Kingdom of Hungary (pre-1918, as part of)
sk.earliestSettlement: Slavic tribes settled the region by the 5th-6th centuries; Great Moravia, centered partly in modern Slovakia, flourished in the 9th century.

keyDates.event: Great Moravia, an early Slavic state, consolidates in the region
Battle of Pressburg: Magyar victory brings about the collapse of Great Moravia
Region becomes part of the Kingdom of Hungary for roughly 900 years
Bratislava (Pressburg) becomes capital and coronation town of Royal Hungary
Czechoslovakia founded, uniting Czechs and Slovaks
Slovak State established as a Nazi German client state
Slovak National Uprising against Nazi occupation
Prague Spring reforms crushed by Warsaw Pact invasion
Peaceful split from Czechoslovakia, Slovakia becomes independent
Slovakia joins the European Union and NATO

sk.climate: Temperate continental, warm summers, cold snowy winters, alpine in the Tatra mountains.
sk.nationalAnimal: Double-barred cross (not animal, symbolic); chamois and brown bear notable in the Tatras

nationalDish.name: Bryndzove halusky (potato dumplings with sheep cheese)

funFacts: Slovakia has more castles and chateaux per capita than any other country in the world.
Bratislava is the only national capital in the world bordering two other countries (Austria and Hungary).
Slovakia produces more cars per capita than any other country in the world.
The Tatra Mountains in Slovakia contain the highest peaks of the Carpathians, including Gerlachovsky stit.
The wooden churches of the Slovak Carpathians are recognized by UNESCO for their construction without a single metal nail.
Slovakia and the Czech Republic were one country, Czechoslovakia, until their peaceful 'Velvet Divorce' split them into two nations in 1993.
Slovakia adopted the euro in 2009, one of the first post-communist Central European states to do so.
Bratislava Castle overlooks the Danube River and has been rebuilt multiple times throughout its history, most recently in the 20th century.

si.earliestSettlement: Slovene tribes settled the region in the 6th century AD; Carantania, an early Slavic principality, formed by the 7th century, one of the oldest Slavic states.

keyDates.event: Principality of Carantania formed, an early Slavic polity
Carantania submits to Bavarian/Frankish overlordship
Region comes under Habsburg rule for nearly 600 years
Joins the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
Axis powers occupy the region during WWII
Becomes a republic within socialist Yugoslavia
Independence from Yugoslavia after a brief Ten-Day War
Joins the European Union and NATO
Adopts the euro, the first post-communist country to do so

si.climate: Alpine in the mountains, continental inland, Mediterranean on the short coast.

unesco.name: Heritage of Mercury - Almaden and Idrija

funFacts: Slovenia is one of the most forested countries in Europe, with trees covering nearly 60% of its territory.
Lake Bled features a tiny island with a church, reachable only by traditional wooden gondola-style boats.
Slovenia was the first former Yugoslav republic to join both the EU and NATO, and to adopt the euro.
Slovenia has more than 10,000 registered caves, including the famous Postojna Cave system explored by electric train since the 19th century.
Ljubljana, Slovenia's capital, was European Green Capital in 2016, known for its pedestrianized riverside center.
Beekeeping is a widespread cultural tradition in Slovenia, with distinctively painted beehive panels serving as a form of folk art.
Triglav, Slovenia's highest peak, is such a national symbol that it appears on the country's flag and coat of arms.
The historic mercury mine at Idrija in Slovenia is one of the oldest of its kind and is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

lt.independence: February 16, 1918 (declared, from Russia/Germany); re-established March 11, 1990, from the Soviet Union
lt.earliestSettlement: Baltic tribes inhabited the region for millennia; the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, founded in the 13th century, became one of the largest states in medieval Europe.

keyDates.event: Mindaugas crowned, founding the Kingdom/Grand Duchy of Lithuania
Grand Duke Jogaila baptized and crowned King of Poland, uniting the two states and Christianizing Lithuania
Polish-Lithuanian forces defeat the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald
Union of Lublin creates the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
Lithuania partitioned, absorbed into the Russian Empire
Independence declared
Soviet occupation and annexation
Nazi Germany occupies Lithuania during Operation Barbarossa
Soviet Red Army reoccupies the country
First Soviet republic to declare restored independence
Soviet troops storm the Vilnius TV tower; independence gains international recognition
Joined the European Union and NATO

lt.climate: Temperate continental/humid continental, cold winters, mild summers.
funFacts: At its height in the 15th century, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania was the largest state in Europe.
Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare restored independence, in March 1990.
Basketball is practically a national religion in Lithuania, with extraordinary per-capita success at the international level.
Vilnius's Old Town is one of the largest surviving medieval old towns in Northern Europe and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Hill of Crosses near Šiauliai holds tens of thousands of crosses planted by pilgrims, a symbol of Lithuanian faith and resistance during Soviet rule.
In 1989, around two million people joined hands to form the 'Baltic Way,' a human chain stretching roughly 675 km through Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia to protest Soviet occupation.
Lithuania was the last pagan country in Europe to convert to Christianity, doing so officially in 1387.
The Lithuanian language is one of the oldest living Indo-European languages, retaining archaic features that linguists consider close to Proto-Indo-European.
Kaunas served as Lithuania's temporary capital between the world wars while Vilnius was under Polish control.
The Lithuanian men's basketball team won bronze medals at three consecutive Olympics (1992, 1996, and 2000).
Lithuania joined the European Union and NATO in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2015.

lv.independence: November 18, 1918 (declared, from Russia/Germany); re-established August 21, 1991, from the Soviet Union
lv.earliestSettlement: Baltic tribes (Latgalians, Couronians, Semigallians, Selonians) settled the region for millennia before German crusaders conquered it in the 13th century, founding Riga in 1201.

keyDates.event: Riga founded by German crusaders/bishop Albert of Riga
Riga joins the Hanseatic League
Livonian Confederation collapses amid the Livonian War
Northern parts come under Russian imperial rule
Final partition of Poland brings the Duchy of Courland under Russian rule
Independence declared
Soviet occupation and annexation
Nazi Germany occupies Latvia during World War II
Soviet Red Army reoccupies the country
Independence restored following the Singing Revolution
Joined the European Union and NATO

famousFeature.name: Riga Old Town / Art Nouveau district

lv.climate: Temperate, maritime-influenced along the coast, more continental inland.
lv.nationalSport: Ice hockey; basketball also very popular
funFacts: Riga has one of the largest and best-preserved collections of Art Nouveau architecture in the world.
Latvia regained independence through the peaceful 'Singing Revolution' of the late 1980s.
The Latvian national song festival, held since 1873, is a UNESCO-recognized intangible cultural tradition involving tens of thousands of singers.
Riga was founded in 1201 and became a major Hanseatic League trading city in the medieval period.
Gauja National Park, Latvia's largest and oldest, is known for its sandstone cliffs, caves, and medieval castles along the Gauja River valley.
Latvia regained independence twice in the 20th century: first in 1918 after World War I, then again in 1991 after Soviet occupation ended.
In 1989, Latvia joined Lithuania and Estonia in the 'Baltic Way,' a roughly 675 km human chain of about two million people protesting Soviet rule.
Midsummer (Jāņi), celebrated on the summer solstice, is Latvia's biggest folk holiday, marked by bonfires, flower crowns, and all-night celebrations.
Forests cover roughly half of Latvia's land, among the highest shares of forest cover in Europe.
Latvia joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2014.

ma.independence: March 2, 1956, from France (Spanish zones also ceded 1956-1958)
ma.earliestSettlement: Berber peoples have inhabited the region since antiquity; the Idrisid dynasty founded the first major Moroccan Islamic state in 788 AD.

keyDates.event: Rome annexes the region as the province of Mauretania Tingitana
Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi reaches the Atlantic, spreading Islam through the region
Idrisid dynasty founds the first Moroccan Islamic state
Almoravid dynasty founds Marrakesh
Almohad dynasty conquers Marrakesh, founding a new empire
Marinid dynasty takes power, ending Almohad rule
Portugal captures Ceuta, beginning European incursions on the coast
Saadi dynasty completes its conquest of Morocco
Battle of the Three Kings: Saadi forces defeat a Portuguese invasion, killing the Portuguese king
Alaouite dynasty founded, the ruling dynasty to the present day
Morocco becomes the first country to recognize US independence
Treaty of Fez establishes French and Spanish protectorates
Independence from France and Spain
Green March asserts control over Western Sahara
Mohammed VI succeeds his father Hassan II as king
Constitutional reforms adopted amid Arab Spring protests
Normalizes diplomatic relations with Israel

ma.climate: Mediterranean in the north, arid in the south/Sahara.
ma.nationalAnimal: Barbary lion (extinct in the wild, historic symbol)
funFacts: Morocco holds roughly three-quarters of the world's known phosphate reserves.
The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859 AD, is recognized by UNESCO and Guinness World Records as the oldest existing degree-granting university in the world.
Morocco's Hassan II Mosque has one of the tallest minarets in the world.
Morocco is the only African country with coastlines on both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea.
The dunes of Erg Chebbi in southeastern Morocco are a major draw for camel trekking into the Sahara.
Casablanca is Morocco's largest city, though the famous 1942 film of the same name was shot almost entirely in Hollywood.
Morocco was the first country to formally recognize United States independence, in 1777.
The medina of Fez al-Bali is one of the largest car-free urban areas in the world, with a maze of narrow streets dating to the 9th century.
Argan oil, prized worldwide in cooking and cosmetics, is produced almost exclusively in Morocco from the nuts of the argan tree.
Morocco's national football team became the first African and Arab team to reach a FIFA World Cup semifinal, in 2022.
Marrakech's Jemaa el-Fnaa square has hosted storytellers, musicians, and food stalls continuously for centuries and is recognized by UNESCO.
ma.territorialNote: Morocco administers most of Western Sahara, a territory whose sovereignty remains disputed, with the Polisario Front seeking independence for the region.

dz.independence: July 5, 1962, from France (after a long war of independence beginning November 1954)
dz.earliestSettlement: Inhabited by Berber peoples since antiquity; came under Carthaginian, Roman, and later Arab-Islamic rule before Ottoman and then French colonization.

keyDates.event: Kingdom of Numidia unified under King Masinissa
Rome destroys Carthage, expands into North Africa
Arab conquest begins, spreading Islam across the region
Ottoman rule established over Algiers
French conquest of Algeria begins
Algerian War of Independence begins
Independence achieved after over a million deaths in the war
Houari Boumédiène seizes power in a coup
Algerian Civil War begins after a cancelled election
Hirak protests force President Bouteflika to resign

dz.climate: Mediterranean along the coast, arid Sahara across most of the south (Algeria is Africa's largest country by area).
funFacts: Algeria is the largest country in Africa by land area.
Over 80% of Algeria's territory is covered by the Sahara Desert.
The Algerian War of Independence (1954-1962) is considered one of the 20th century's most significant anti-colonial conflicts.
Algeria holds some of the largest proven natural gas reserves in the world.
The Tassili n'Ajjer plateau contains thousands of prehistoric rock paintings and engravings, some dating back over 10,000 years.
Nobel Prize-winning writer Albert Camus was born in French Algeria and set much of his fiction there.
Algiers is nicknamed 'Alger la Blanche' ('Algiers the White') for the whitewashed buildings of its old Ottoman-era quarter, the Casbah.
Rai music, a popular genre blending traditional Algerian sounds with Western influences, originated in the city of Oran.
Some towns in the Algerian Sahara, such as In Salah, record some of the highest average temperatures on Earth.

tn.earliestSettlement: Carthage, founded by Phoenician settlers around 814 BC near modern Tunis, became one of the great powers of the ancient Mediterranean before its destruction by Rome in 146 BC.

keyDates.event: Carthage founded by Phoenician settlers (traditional date)
Rome destroys Carthage in the Third Punic War
Vandals capture Carthage
Byzantine Empire reconquers the region
Arab conquest; Kairouan founded as a center of Islamic learning
Ottoman rule established
France establishes a protectorate over Tunisia
Independence from France
Habib Bourguiba abolishes the monarchy, becomes first president
Zine El Abidine Ben Ali ousts Bourguiba in a bloodless coup
Tunisian Revolution ousts Ben Ali, sparking the wider Arab Spring
President Kais Saied suspends parliament, consolidating power

tn.climate: Mediterranean in the north, arid/Saharan in the south.
tn.nationalAnimal: Eagle (featured on the coat of arms)
funFacts: Tunisia sparked the Arab Spring in 2011, the only country from that wave to transition to a sustained democracy for over a decade.
Ancient Carthage, near modern Tunis, was once Rome's greatest rival for control of the Mediterranean.
Star Wars' fictional planet Tatooine was named after the real Tunisian town of Tataouine, where parts of the films were shot.
Tunisia's El Jem Amphitheatre is one of the best-preserved Roman amphitheaters in the world, rivaling the Colosseum in scale.
The Great Mosque of Kairouan, founded in 670 AD, is considered one of the oldest and most important mosques in the Islamic world.
Tunisia is the northernmost country in Africa, with Cape Angela (Ras ben Sakka) marking the continent's most northerly point.
Harissa, a spicy chili paste, is a staple condiment of Tunisian cuisine.
Tunisia was the first Arab country to abolish slavery, in 1846.

government.form: Transitional/divided governance (no single unified government since 2014)

ly.earliestSettlement: The coast was settled by Phoenicians and Greeks in antiquity (Leptis Magna, Cyrene); came under Ottoman rule before Italian colonization from 1911.

keyDates.event: Greek colony of Cyrene founded
Rome annexes Cyrenaica as a province
Arab conquest brings Islam to the region
Ottoman Empire captures Tripoli, beginning centuries of Ottoman rule
Italy invades and colonizes Libya
Allied forces take control of Libya from Italy during World War II
Independence as the United Kingdom of Libya
Muammar Gaddafi seizes power in a coup
Libyan Civil War topples and kills Gaddafi; ongoing instability follows
Second civil war begins, splitting the country between rival governments
Ceasefire agreement signed, ending major fighting

ly.climate: Mediterranean along the coast, arid Sahara across most of the interior.
funFacts: Libya has Africa's largest proven oil reserves.
Leptis Magna is considered one of the best-preserved Roman ruins in the Mediterranean.
Libya built the Great Man-Made River, once the world's largest irrigation project, to pipe fossil water from aquifers beneath the Sahara to coastal cities.
Over 90% of Libya's land is classified as desert or semi-desert, mostly part of the Sahara.
Libya gained independence in 1951 as the United Kingdom of Libya, becoming the first country to achieve independence through the United Nations.
The ancient city of Cyrene, founded by Greek colonists around 630 BC, was once one of the principal cities of the Hellenic world.
Libya has the longest Mediterranean coastline of any African country.
Berber (Amazigh) communities in Libya, particularly in the Nafusa Mountains, maintain distinct languages and traditions that predate Arab settlement.
The Tadrart Acacus mountains in Libya's southwest feature prehistoric rock art thousands of years old, depicting a once-green Sahara filled with wildlife.

gh.independence: March 6, 1957, from the United Kingdom (first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence)
gh.earliestSettlement: Home to powerful pre-colonial states including the Ashanti Empire, which rose to prominence in the 17th-18th centuries through control of gold and trade routes.

keyDates.event: Portuguese build Elmina Castle, beginning European trade on the Gold Coast
Ashanti Empire begins its rise to regional dominance
Gold Coast becomes a formal British colony
Independence - first sub-Saharan African country to gain it from colonial rule
Becomes a republic under President Kwame Nkrumah
First of several military coups following independence
Jerry Rawlings seizes power in a second coup
Return to stable multi-party democracy
First peaceful transfer of power between political parties

gh.climate: Tropical, hot and humid along the coast, drier savanna in the north.
gh.nationalAnimal: Black star (symbolic); the eagle also features on the coat of arms

unesco.name: Forts and Castles, Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions

funFacts: Ghana was the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from colonial rule, in 1957.
Ghana is the world's second-largest producer of cocoa, after Ivory Coast.
The Akosombo Dam created Lake Volta, one of the largest man-made lakes in the world by surface area.
Ghana was formerly known as the Gold Coast under British colonial rule, named for its historic gold trade.
The Ashanti Empire was one of the most powerful West African states, famed for its goldwork and the Golden Stool, a sacred royal symbol.
Independence Square in Accra, also known as Black Star Square, is one of the largest city squares in the world.
Jollof rice, a spiced rice dish, is a beloved staple across Ghana and the subject of a long-running friendly rivalry with Nigeria.
Cape Coast Castle, a former slave-trading post on Ghana's coast, is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and museum.
Ghana is home to more than 100 ethnic groups, including the Akan, Ewe, and Ga.

sn.earliestSettlement: Home to ancient trading kingdoms; the island of Goree became a major hub of the Atlantic slave trade from the 15th-19th centuries.

keyDates.event: Jolof Empire founded, uniting Wolof kingdoms (approx.)
Portuguese reach the Senegal coast, beginning European contact
French found Saint-Louis, their first permanent West African settlement
France captures Goree Island from the Dutch, a major slave-trade hub
Dakar founded as French colonial expansion continues under Louis Faidherbe
Senegal becomes part of French West Africa
Independence from France
First peaceful democratic transfer of power
Macky Sall elected president

sn.climate: Tropical, hot with a dry season and a rainy season.
sn.nationalSport: Senegalese wrestling (laamb); football also hugely popular
funFacts: Goree Island, off the coast of Dakar, is a major memorial site of the trans-Atlantic slave trade and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Senegal is regarded as one of Africa's more stable democracies, with no successful coups since independence.
Senegal was a founding leader of the Negritude cultural and political movement through poet-president Leopold Senghor.
Senegal is home to Lake Retba (Lac Rose), famous for its pink-tinted waters caused by salt-loving algae.
Dakar, Senegal's capital, is the westernmost major city on the African mainland.
Senegalese wrestling (laamb), which combines traditional combat with ritual and music, is the country's most popular spectator sport.
The Paris-Dakar Rally, one of the world's most grueling off-road races, was historically named for its finish line in Senegal's capital before the event moved to South America in 2009.
Senegal is known for its vibrant djembe drumming and griot oral storytelling traditions, passed down through generations of hereditary musicians.
Senegal's Casamance region, south of the Gambia, is known for its lush rice-growing wetlands, distinct from the drier Sahelian north.
sn.currencyNote: Senegal uses the West African CFA franc, a shared currency pegged to the euro and used by eight West African countries.

ci.earliestSettlement: Various kingdoms and chieftaincies predated French colonization, including the Kong Empire; became a key French West African colony focused on cash-crop agriculture.

keyDates.event: Kong Empire founded, a major Islamic trading state in the north (approx.)
France signs treaties establishing protectorates along the coast
Ivory Coast becomes a French colony
Independence from France under Félix Houphouët-Boigny
Yamoussoukro officially becomes the capital (though Abidjan remains the economic hub)
First military coup ends decades of political stability
Civil war breaks out, splitting the country north-south
Post-election crisis and violence following disputed 2010 vote

famousFeature.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, Yamoussoukro

ci.climate: Tropical, hot and humid along the coast, drier savanna in the north.
ci.nationalAnimal: Elephant (the country's name itself references the historic ivory trade)
funFacts: Ivory Coast is the world's largest producer of cocoa, supplying around 40% of the global crop.
The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in Yamoussoukro is one of the largest church buildings in the world, modeled on St. Peter's Basilica.
Ivory Coast's official capital is Yamoussoukro, but Abidjan remains the de facto economic and administrative center.
Ivory Coast gained independence from France in 1960.
Football star Didier Drogba became a symbol of national unity during the country's period of civil conflict.
Ivory Coast's economy relies heavily on agricultural exports, including cocoa, coffee and palm oil.
The country experienced two civil wars in the 2000s before stabilizing in the following decade.
Ivory Coast takes its English name from the historic ivory trade once conducted along its coast.
ci.currencyNote: Ivory Coast uses the West African CFA franc, a shared currency pegged to the euro and used by several West African countries.

cm.independence: January 1, 1960, from France (French Cameroon); British Southern Cameroons joined later in 1961
cm.earliestSettlement: Home to diverse kingdoms including the Sao civilization near Lake Chad and the Bamum Kingdom, before German colonization from 1884, later split between France and Britain after WWI.

keyDates.event: Bamum Kingdom founded in the west (later known for King Njoya's invented script)
Portuguese explorers reach the coast and name it Rio dos Camarões, giving the country its name
Germany establishes the colony of Kamerun
League of Nations splits Cameroon between France and Britain after WWI
French Cameroun gains independence
British Southern Cameroons joins to form a federal republic
Federal system replaced by a unitary state
Anglophone crisis begins in the English-speaking regions

cm.climate: Highly varied, often called 'Africa in miniature' - tropical coast, savanna north, highlands.
funFacts: Cameroon is nicknamed 'Africa in miniature' for its wide range of climates, landscapes and cultures packed into one country.
Cameroon is one of the few African countries with both French and English as official languages, a legacy of its split colonial history.
The Indomitable Lions' 1990 World Cup run was the first time an African team reached the quarterfinals.
Mount Cameroon, an active volcano, is the highest peak in West Africa.
Cameroon is home to more than 250 ethnic groups and around 250 languages, making it one of the most linguistically diverse countries in Africa.
Cameroonian musician Manu Dibango's 1972 hit 'Soul Makossa' helped influence the development of disco music.
Cameroon gained independence from France in 1960, and the British-administered Southern Cameroons joined shortly after via referendum.
Cameroon's name comes from the Portuguese word 'camaroes' (prawns), after the abundant shrimp early explorers found in the Wouri River estuary.
cm.currencyNote: Cameroon uses the Central African CFA franc, a shared currency pegged to the euro and used by six Central African countries.

cl.earliestSettlement: Indigenous Mapuche peoples resisted Inca and later Spanish conquest for centuries; Santiago was founded by Pedro de Valdivia in 1541.

keyDates.event: Inca Empire extends its frontier into northern Chile (approx.)
Pedro de Valdivia founds Santiago
Arauco War begins; Mapuche resistance delays Spanish conquest of the south for centuries
First steps toward independence from Spain
Independence formally secured
War of the Pacific begins, Chile gains mineral-rich northern territories
Military coup brings Augusto Pinochet to power
Return to democracy after 17 years of dictatorship
Michelle Bachelet becomes Chile's first female president
Mass protests over inequality trigger a constitutional reform process

cl.climate: Extremely varied given its length - the Atacama Desert in the north, Mediterranean in the center, cold and wet in the south.
cl.nationalAnimal: Andean condor and huemul deer (both on the coat of arms)
cl.nationalSport: Chilean rodeo (official); football most widely followed

unesco.name: Historic Quarter of the Seaport City of Valparaiso

funFacts: Chile is the world's largest producer of copper and a major lithium producer.
Chile is one of the longest and narrowest countries in the world, stretching over 4,300 km north to south.
Easter Island, famous for its moai statues, is a remote Chilean territory in the Pacific.
Chile's Atacama Desert is one of the driest places on Earth, with some weather stations having never recorded rainfall.
Chile's clear, dry northern skies make it home to some of the world's premier astronomical observatories.
Chile is one of the world's largest wine exporters.
The 2010 rescue of 33 trapped Chilean miners after 69 days underground drew global attention.
Chile consistently ranks among the highest in Latin America on the Human Development Index.
Valparaiso's historic funiculars and colorful hillside houses form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

ve.earliestSettlement: Indigenous peoples inhabited the region for thousands of years; Spanish colonization began with the founding of Cumana in 1521, one of the oldest continuously inhabited European settlements in the Americas.

keyDates.event: Columbus reaches the Venezuelan coast on his third voyage
Spanish found Cumana, one of the oldest European settlements in the Americas
Declaration of independence
Venezuela separates from Gran Colombia
Juan Vicente Gomez begins a long dictatorship (ends 1935)
Major oil discovery transforms the Venezuelan economy
Democracy established after dictator Marcos Perez Jimenez is overthrown
Hugo Chavez becomes president, beginning the 'Bolivarian Revolution'
Chavez dies; Nicolas Maduro succeeds him amid deepening economic crisis
Political crisis deepens as Juan Guaido declares himself interim president

ve.climate: Tropical, varying from humid lowlands to cooler Andean highlands.
funFacts: Venezuela holds the world's largest proven oil reserves.
Angel Falls, in Venezuela, is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall at 979 m.
Venezuela has won more Miss Universe and Miss World titles than almost any other country.
Venezuela was one of the founding members of OPEC in 1960.
Where the Catatumbo River meets Lake Maracaibo, the sky produces one of the world's most frequent lightning displays, known as the Catatumbo lightning.
Venezuela's flat-topped tepui mountains, including Mount Roraima, are thought to have inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's novel 'The Lost World.'
Baseball is hugely popular in Venezuela, which has produced many stars of Major League Baseball.
Venezuela gained independence from Spain in 1821, with Simon Bolivar playing a central role in the struggle.
ve.currencyNote: Venezuela experienced one of the worst hyperinflation episodes in modern history during the 2010s, forcing multiple redenominations of the bolívar to remove excess zeros.
ve.territorialNote: Venezuela claims the Essequibo region, which makes up roughly two-thirds of neighboring Guyana's territory, in a long-running border dispute.

ec.independence: May 24, 1822 (Battle of Pichincha secures independence from Spain, as part of Gran Colombia); fully sovereign 1830
ec.earliestSettlement: Home to numerous indigenous cultures before incorporation into the Inca Empire in the 15th century; Quito, the capital, has pre-Columbian roots over 1,000 years old.

keyDates.event: Incas conquer the Kingdom of Quito
Spanish conquest and founding of Quito as a Spanish city
Royal Audiencia of Quito established under the Spanish Empire
First call for independence in Quito
Battle of Pichincha secures independence
Ecuador becomes a fully sovereign state after leaving Gran Colombia
War with Peru over border disputes (recurs until a 1998 peace treaty)
Return to democratic civilian rule after military dictatorship
Adopts the US dollar as official currency amid economic crisis
New constitution adopted

ec.climate: Highly varied - tropical coast and Amazon, temperate Andean highlands.
ec.nationalSport: Ecuavoley (a local volleyball variant); football most widely followed
funFacts: Due to the equatorial bulge, the summit of Chimborazo is the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's center.
Ecuador was the first country in the world to officially codify the Rights of Nature into its constitution, in 2008.
Charles Darwin's observations on the Galapagos Islands, part of Ecuador, were central to his theory of evolution.
Ecuador is named after the equator, which runs directly through the country, including a monument just north of Quito.
The traditional straw hat known worldwide as the 'Panama hat' is actually woven in Ecuador, not Panama.
Ecuador adopted the US dollar as its official currency in 2000, abandoning its own currency, the sucre.
The historic centre of Quito was among the very first sites ever inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, in 1978.
Despite its small size, Ecuador is one of the most biodiverse countries on Earth, home to thousands of species of plants, birds and amphibians.

funFacts: Bolivia holds the world's largest reserves of lithium, a key resource for batteries.
The Salar de Uyuni, the world's largest salt flat, turns into a vast mirror during the rainy season.
Bolivia has two capitals: Sucre (constitutional) and La Paz (seat of government), with La Paz the highest capital city in the world by elevation.
Bolivia is named after independence leader Simon Bolivar.
The silver mines of Cerro Rico in Potosi helped fund the Spanish Empire for centuries and once made Potosi one of the largest cities in the world.
Lake Titicaca, shared with Peru, is the highest navigable lake in the world.
Bolivia is one of only two landlocked countries in South America, having lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879-1884).
Bolivia recognizes 37 official languages, more than any other country, reflecting its many indigenous peoples.
The ancient Tiwanaku civilization, which predated the Inca, built monumental stone structures near Lake Titicaca.
Salteñas, a baked pastry filled with meat or vegetables in a sweet-savory sauce, are a beloved Bolivian snack.
bo.currencyNote: Bolivia suffered one of history's worst hyperinflations in the mid-1980s, resolved by introducing the boliviano in 1987 to replace the old peso boliviano.
bo.territorialNote: Bolivia has been landlocked since losing its Pacific coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884), a status it has long disputed.

Guarani is a co-official language alongside Spanish, spoken by the majority of the population.
Asuncion, Paraguay's capital, is one of the oldest cities in South America, founded in 1537.

Nandutí, a delicate spider-web-patterned lace, is a celebrated traditional Paraguayan handicraft.
The ruins of the Jesuit Missions of La Santisima Trinidad de Parana and Jesus de Tavarangue in Paraguay are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
The harp is considered Paraguay's national instrument and is central to its folk music tradition.

Uruguay was among the first countries in the world to fully legalize and regulate the production and sale of cannabis, in 2013.
Uruguay generates nearly all of its electricity from renewable sources, mostly wind and hydro.
Uruguay is one of the most secular countries in Latin America, having formally separated church and state in 1917.
Montevideo, Uruguay's capital, is home to more than half the country's total population.

Gaucho (cowboy) traditions remain an important part of Uruguayan rural culture and national identity.
Punta del Este, a resort town on Uruguay's coast, is known for its beaches and modern architecture, including the famous 'Hand' sculpture.
Uruguay has one of the highest per-capita rates of mate, a caffeinated herbal infusion, consumption in the world.

The US trade embargo on Cuba, in place since the early 1960s, is one of the longest-running in modern history.
Cuba's classic American cars from the 1950s, kept running for decades due to the embargo, have become a symbol of the country.
Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean.
Cuban cigars, especially from the Pinar del Rio region, are considered among the finest in the world.
Havana's historic center is a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its Spanish colonial architecture.
Cuba has a widely regarded medical training system and has sent doctors abroad on medical missions to dozens of countries.
Baseball is immensely popular in Cuba, and the country has produced many Major League Baseball stars.
The 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion, a failed US-backed attempt to overthrow Fidel Castro's government, remains a defining moment in Cuban history.

Dominoes and cricket are hugely popular pastimes across Jamaica, reflecting British colonial influence.
Jamaica is the third-largest island in the Caribbean by area.
Ska and rocksteady, music genres that developed in Jamaica in the 1950s and 60s, were direct precursors to reggae.

The Yemeni island of Socotra, in the Arabian Sea, is home to many plant species found nowhere else on Earth, including the distinctive dragon's blood tree.
Yemen is traditionally considered an original home of coffee cultivation, and the port city of Mocha lent its name to the coffee variety.
Sana'a, Yemen's capital, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, with a UNESCO-listed old city of distinctive tower houses.
Yemen was divided into North Yemen and South Yemen until the two unified in 1990.
ye.currencyNote: Since 2016, Yemen's civil conflict has produced two competing exchange rates for its rial, issued by rival central banks based in Sana'a and Aden.

government.form: Unitary Islamic emirate (de facto, under Taliban rule since 2021)

Greco-Bactrian Kingdom emerges as a Hellenistic successor state (approx.)
Arab conquest brings Islam to the region (approx.)
Genghis Khan's Mongol invasion devastates the region
Babur captures Kabul, a base for the future Mughal Empire
Ahmad Shah Durrani founds the Durrani Empire, considered the founding of modern Afghanistan
First Anglo-Afghan War begins with a British invasion
Second Anglo-Afghan War begins

Full independence following the Third Anglo-Afghan War

Soviet invasion begins a decade-long war
Soviet forces withdraw
Taliban capture Kabul and establish their first regime
US-led invasion topples the Taliban after the September 11 attacks
Taliban retakes control after the withdrawal of US/NATO forces

af.climate: Arid continental, hot summers, cold winters, alpine in the mountains.
naturalResources: Lithium and rare earth minerals (largely untapped)

unesco.name: Minaret and Archaeological Remains of Jam
Cultural Landscape and Archaeological Remains of the Bamiyan Valley

funFacts: The Bamiyan Buddhas, giant ancient statues carved into cliffs, were destroyed by the Taliban in 2001 but remain a major cultural memory site.
Afghanistan sits on an estimated trillion dollars or more in untapped mineral wealth, including lithium.
Buzkashi, Afghanistan's national sport, involves horseback riders competing to drag a goat carcass to a goal.
Afghanistan is home to the Wakhan Corridor, a narrow mountainous strip of land that extends all the way to the Chinese border.
Kabul has been continuously inhabited for more than 3,500 years, making it one of the oldest cities in Asia.
The Khyber Pass, linking Afghanistan and Pakistan, has served as a key trade and invasion route for thousands of years.
Afghanistan is landlocked, bordered by six countries: Pakistan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and a narrow strip touching China.
Lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan's Badakhshan region has been traded for over 6,000 years and was ground into the ultramarine pigment used by Renaissance painters.
Afghanistan has been home to successive ancient empires, including the Greco-Bactrians, Mauryans, and Mongols, leaving a rich layered archaeological record.
The Minaret of Jam, a 12th-century tower in a remote valley, is one of the few structures to survive largely intact from the Ghurid dynasty.
af.territorialNote: Afghanistan does not formally recognize the Durand Line, drawn by the British in 1893, as its border with Pakistan.

ug.earliestSettlement: Home to several pre-colonial kingdoms, most notably the Kingdom of Buganda, one of the oldest and most powerful states in the African Great Lakes region.

keyDates.event: Kingdom of Buganda founded (approx.)
John Hanning Speke becomes the first European to document the source of the Nile at Lake Victoria
Britain establishes the Uganda Protectorate
Independence from Britain
Idi Amin seizes power in a coup, begins brutal dictatorship
Amin expels the country's Asian population
Amin overthrown following a Tanzanian-backed invasion
Yoweri Museveni takes power after a guerrilla war
Lord's Resistance Army insurgency begins in northern Uganda

ug.climate: Tropical, moderated by altitude; relatively mild for its equatorial location.

unesco.name: Tombs of Buganda Kings at Kasubi

funFacts: Uganda is home to roughly half of the world's remaining mountain gorilla population.
Winston Churchill famously nicknamed Uganda the 'Pearl of Africa' for its lush landscapes.
The source of the River Nile, the world's longest river, is traditionally located at Jinja, Uganda, on Lake Victoria.
Uganda straddles the equator, marked by monuments visitors can stand astride near Kayabwe.
Lake Victoria, Africa's largest lake by surface area, is shared between Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania.
Uganda gained independence from Britain in 1962.
The Rwenzori Mountains, nicknamed the 'Mountains of the Moon,' have glaciers despite sitting almost on the equator.
Ugandan runner Stephen Kiprotich won Olympic gold in the marathon at the 2012 London Games.
Uganda has one of the youngest populations of any country, with a median age under 17.
Kampala, Uganda's capital, is traditionally said to be built across seven hills.

tz.independence: December 9, 1961, Tanganyika (from the UK); Zanzibar January 12, 1964; merged as Tanzania April 26, 1964
tz.earliestSettlement: The Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania is one of the most important paleoanthropological sites in the world, with hominid fossils dating back nearly 2 million years.

Vasco da Gama reaches the Swahili coast
Omani Arabs expel the Portuguese from the Swahili coast
Omani Sultan Seyyid Said moves his capital to Zanzibar, building it into a hub of the slave and spice trade

Arusha Declaration establishes Ujamaa socialist policy under Nyerere

Constitution amended to permit multiparty politics

tz.climate: Varied - tropical coast, temperate highlands, arid interior plateaus.
majorReligions: Islam (particularly strong on the coast and Zanzibar)
funFacts: Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's tallest peak, is the highest freestanding mountain in the world.
Tanzanite, the rare blue-violet gemstone, is found in commercial quantities only near Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania.
The Serengeti hosts the largest terrestrial mammal migration on Earth, with over a million wildebeest.
The Ngorongoro Crater is the world's largest inactive, intact volcanic caldera and teems with wildlife year-round.
Zanzibar, part of Tanzania, was historically a major center of the Indian Ocean spice and slave trade and is still known today as the 'Spice Island.'
Tanzania was formed in 1964 through the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar, giving the country its name (TAN-ZAN-ia).
Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania is one of the most important paleoanthropological sites in the world, where fossils have shed light on early human evolution.
Swahili, now widely spoken across East Africa, developed along the coast of Tanzania and Zanzibar through centuries of Bantu and Arab trade contact.

zm.earliestSettlement: Home to various Bantu-speaking peoples who migrated into the region over the past 2,000 years; became a British protectorate as Northern Rhodesia in 1924.

keyDates.event: David Livingstone becomes the first European to see Victoria Falls
Cecil Rhodes' British South Africa Company begins establishing control

Northern Rhodesia joins the Central African Federation
Independence as Zambia under Kenneth Kaunda
One-party state declared under Kaunda
First multi-party elections after one-party rule
Peaceful transfer of power following opposition election win

zm.climate: Tropical/subtropical, moderated by altitude, with a distinct dry season.
funFacts: Victoria Falls, shared with Zimbabwe, is known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'The Smoke That Thunders.'
Zambia is one of Africa's largest copper producers, with the metal central to its economy for over a century.
Zambia is home to over 70 distinct ethnic groups, each with its own language and traditions.
Zambia gained independence from Britain in 1964, led by its first president, Kenneth Kaunda.
South Luangwa National Park is renowned for its walking safaris, a format pioneered in Zambia.
Zambia is landlocked and shares borders with eight other countries.
The Zambezi River, Africa's fourth-longest river, flows through Zambia and forms Victoria Falls on its border with Zimbabwe.

zw.independence: April 18, 1980, from the United Kingdom (following the Rhodesian Bush War)
zw.earliestSettlement: Home to the Great Zimbabwe civilization, a powerful medieval kingdom that built the massive stone ruins the modern country is named after, flourishing from the 11th-15th centuries.

zw.climate: Tropical, moderated by altitude, with a distinct dry season.
zw.nationalAnimal: Zimbabwe bird (stylized on the flag and coat of arms)
funFacts: The country takes its name from Great Zimbabwe, the medieval stone city whose ruins remain the largest ancient structure in sub-Saharan Africa south of the Sahara.
Zimbabwe experienced one of the worst hyperinflation episodes in modern history in the late 2000s.
Victoria Falls, on Zimbabwe's border with Zambia, is one of the largest waterfalls in the world by combined width and height.
Zimbabwe was formerly known as Rhodesia before gaining independence in 1980.
Hwange National Park is Zimbabwe's largest game reserve, home to large populations of elephants.
Zimbabwe largely abandoned its own currency in 2009, turning to foreign currencies such as the US dollar after hyperinflation made the Zimbabwean dollar nearly worthless.
The soapstone 'Zimbabwe Bird,' found among the Great Zimbabwe ruins, is a national emblem depicted on the country's flag.
zw.currencyNote: Zimbabwe suffered one of the worst hyperinflation episodes in history in the late 2000s, peaking in 2008, which led it to abandon its own currency in favor of foreign currencies including the US dollar.

mz.earliestSettlement: Swahili trading settlements dotted the coast for centuries before Vasco da Gama's arrival in 1498 opened the region to Portuguese colonization.

mz.climate: Tropical to subtropical, with a wet and dry season.
funFacts: Mozambique's name comes from the Island of Mozambique, once the Portuguese colonial capital of the entire territory.
Mozambique is home to large untapped natural gas reserves that are reshaping its economy.
The country's long civil war (1977-1992) was one of Africa's most devastating conflicts, killing roughly a million people.
Mozambique's coastline stretches over 2,500 km along the Indian Ocean, among the longest in Africa.
The Bazaruto Archipelago off Mozambique's coast is known for its coral reefs and is one of the last refuges of the dugong in the western Indian Ocean.
Mozambique joined the Commonwealth of Nations in 1995, despite never having been a British colony.
Portuguese is Mozambique's official language, a legacy of more than 400 years of colonial rule.
Cashew nuts were once Mozambique's dominant export before the civil war disrupted production.

mg.earliestSettlement: Settled by Austronesian seafarers from present-day Indonesia roughly 1,500-2,000 years ago, giving Madagascar a unique blend of Southeast Asian and African cultural heritage.

Political crisis leads to a change of government

mg.nationalSport: Football (soccer); traditional moraingy (martial art) also notable
funFacts: Over 90% of Madagascar's wildlife is found nowhere else on Earth, including all lemur species.
Madagascar produces most of the world's natural vanilla.
Madagascar split from the African mainland over 150 million years ago, allowing its unique species to evolve in isolation.
Madagascar is the fourth-largest island in the world, after Greenland, New Guinea, and Borneo.
More than 100 species of lemur are found only on Madagascar and a few surrounding islands.
The Avenue of the Baobabs features trees estimated to be over 800 years old and is one of Madagascar's most iconic landmarks.
Madagascar was ruled by a series of powerful Merina monarchs before becoming a French colony in 1897, then regaining independence in 1960.
Rice is eaten at nearly every meal in Madagascar, giving the country one of the highest per-capita rice consumption rates in the world.
Famadihana, or 'turning of the bones,' is a traditional Malagasy funerary custom in which families exhume ancestors' remains, rewrap them, and dance with them in celebration.

Independence as Botswana, one of Africa's poorest countries at the time

Botswana recognized as one of Africa's most stable democracies and economies

naturalResources: Diamonds (one of the world's largest producers)
funFacts: Botswana transformed from one of the world's poorest countries at independence into one of Africa's most stable and prosperous democracies, largely through careful management of diamond wealth.
The Okavango Delta is one of the few major inland river deltas that never reaches the sea, instead spreading into the Kalahari Desert.
Botswana has one of the largest elephant populations of any country in the world.
Much of Botswana is covered by the Kalahari Desert, making it one of the least densely populated countries on Earth.
The Central Kalahari Game Reserve in Botswana is one of the largest protected wildlife areas in the world.
Botswana follows a 'low-volume, high-value' tourism model aimed at protecting its wildlife and ecosystems.
Diamonds, discovered shortly after independence in 1966, transformed Botswana's economy through a revenue-sharing partnership between the government and De Beers.
The San (Bushmen) peoples, among the oldest continuous cultures in the world, have long inhabited the Kalahari region of Botswana.
Botswana has never experienced a coup and is often cited as one of Africa's most consistent multiparty democracies since independence.

na.climate: Arid to semi-arid; the Namib is one of the world's oldest and driest deserts.
funFacts: The Namib Desert, after which the country is named, is considered one of the oldest deserts in the world.
Namibia was the first country in the world to incorporate environmental protection into its constitution.
Namibia has one of the lowest population densities of any country on Earth.
Namibia gained independence from South Africa in 1990, one of the last African countries to do so.
Namibia's Skeleton Coast is named for the shipwrecks and whale bones that litter its shores.
Namibia is home to the largest free-roaming population of cheetahs in the world.
The Himba people of northern Namibia are known for covering their skin in a mixture of butterfat and ochre, giving it a distinctive reddish hue.
Namibia has significant deposits of diamonds and uranium, both important to its economy.
na.currencyNote: The Namibian dollar is pegged 1:1 to the South African rand, which also circulates as legal tender in Namibia.

Lake Malawi contains more fish species than any other lake in the world, including hundreds of unique cichlid species.
Malawi is one of the most densely populated countries in Africa despite being relatively small.
Malawi was known as Nyasaland under British colonial rule before gaining independence in 1964.
Lake Malawi, Africa's third-largest lake, makes up roughly a fifth of the country's total area.
Chichewa and English are Malawi's official languages, alongside more than a dozen other spoken languages.
Malawi's economy relies heavily on agriculture, particularly tobacco, since it lacks the mineral wealth of many neighboring countries.
The Nyika Plateau in northern Malawi is known for its rolling highland grasslands, unusual scenery for the region.

rw.earliestSettlement: Home to a centuries-old Tutsi-led kingdom before German and then Belgian colonization, which hardened ethnic divisions that later contributed to immense tragedy.

funFacts: Rwanda is known as the 'Land of a Thousand Hills' for its mountainous terrain.

Rwanda has one of the highest proportions of women in parliament of any country in the world.
Rwanda is home to roughly a third of the world's remaining mountain gorillas, protected in Volcanoes National Park.
Rwanda holds a monthly national day of community service called Umuganda, when citizens join together for public work projects.
Kigali, Rwanda's capital, is regularly ranked among the cleanest and safest cities in Africa.
Coffee and tea grown in Rwanda's volcanic highlands are prized globally for their high quality.
Gorilla trekking permits in Rwanda are among the most expensive wildlife permits in the world, with proceeds funding conservation.

Mongolia is one of the least densely populated countries on Earth, with vast open steppe still used for nomadic herding.
Ulaanbaatar is the coldest national capital city in the world by average annual temperature.
Mongolia has the lowest population density of any independent country, with roughly two people per square kilometer.
The Naadam festival, held every July, celebrates Mongolia's 'three manly games' — wrestling, horse racing, and archery — a tradition dating back centuries.
Roughly a quarter to a third of Mongolians still live a nomadic or semi-nomadic herding lifestyle, moving seasonally between pastures in traditional round tents called gers.
The Gobi Desert, spanning much of southern Mongolia, has yielded some of the world's most significant dinosaur fossil discoveries, including fossilized dinosaur eggs.
Mongolia transitioned peacefully from Communist rule to a multi-party democracy in 1990.

np.earliestSettlement: The Kathmandu Valley has been continuously settled for over 2,000 years; Nepal is the birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha), born in Lumbini around the 6th century BC.

Nepal was never colonized by a European power.
Nepal's flag is the only national flag in the world that is not a rectangle or square - it's made of two overlapping triangular pennants.
Nepal is traditionally regarded as the birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, born in Lumbini around the 6th century BCE.
Kathmandu's Durbar Square and several other sites in the Kathmandu Valley are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
The Gurkhas, renowned Nepali soldiers, have served in the British and Indian armies for over two centuries.
Nepal is home to a highly diverse population, with more than 120 languages spoken across the country.
Mount Everest grows a few millimeters taller most years because of ongoing tectonic activity.

bd.earliestSettlement: The Bengal region has a civilizational history stretching back thousands of years, with the ancient Pundra and Gangaridai kingdoms among the earliest recorded states.

Pala Empire founded, a major Buddhist dynasty centered in Bengal
Muslim conquest of Bengal begins

Bangladesh has one of the highest population densities of any sizable country in the world.
Bangladesh is a world leader in ready-made garment exports, second only to China.
Bangladesh is largely formed by the Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta, the largest river delta on Earth.
Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh has one of the longest unbroken natural sea beaches in the world.
Jute, once called 'the golden fibre,' made Bengal a historic center of the global textile trade.
Bangladesh's 1971 Liberation War secured its independence from Pakistan after a nine-month conflict.
Dhaka is sometimes called the 'rickshaw capital of the world' for the sheer number of cycle rickshaws on its streets.

lk.earliestSettlement: Anuradhapura, founded around the 4th century BC, became the capital of one of the longest-lasting continuous monarchies in the world, lasting over 1,300 years.

Buddhism introduced to the island by Mahinda, son of Emperor Ashoka
King Dutugemunu reunifies the island under Anuradhapura rule
Chola dynasty of South India conquers the Anuradhapura Kingdom

funFacts: Sri Lanka was the first country in the world to elect a woman as head of government, Sirimavo Bandaranaike, in 1960.
Sigiriya, an ancient rock fortress, features frescoes and engineering dating back to the 5th century AD.
Sri Lanka is one of the world's leading tea-exporting countries, famous for 'Ceylon tea.'
Sri Lanka was known as Ceylon until it adopted its current name in 1972.

The Sri Maha Bodhi tree in Anuradhapura, grown from a cutting of the original tree under which the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment, was planted around 288 BC and is one of the oldest documented trees in the world.
Adam's Peak, a 2,243-meter mountain, is a pilgrimage site held sacred by Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims, and Christians alike.
Cricket is Sri Lanka's most popular sport; the national team won the Cricket World Cup in 1996.
Sri Lanka was one of the earliest sources of cinnamon in the ancient world, and 'Ceylon cinnamon' is still prized as 'true cinnamon.'
Ancient Sri Lankan kings built vast irrigation reservoirs, known as 'tanks,' over 2,000 years ago, many of which are still in use today.
Sri Lanka has eight UNESCO World Heritage Sites, including the ancient cities of Polonnaruwa and Anuradhapura.
