funFacts: Bagan contains over 2,000 surviving Buddhist temples and pagodas from its medieval golden age, one of the richest archaeological sites in Southeast Asia.
Myanmar is one of the world's leading sources of jade and rubies.
Myanmar has had two official names in recent history - Burma and Myanmar - a change adopted by the military government in 1989 that remains politically contested.
Myanmar is the world's largest exporter of teak wood.
The Irrawaddy River, Myanmar's most important waterway, flows the length of the country from the Himalayas to the Andaman Sea.
Nearly 90% of Myanmar's population practices Theravada Buddhism, and the country has tens of thousands of active pagodas and monasteries.
The Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon, said to enshrine relics of the Buddha, is covered in hundreds of kilograms of gold leaf and is Myanmar's most sacred Buddhist site.
Myanmar is home to more than 100 distinct ethnic groups, including the Bamar majority alongside Shan, Karen, Kachin, and many others.

kh.earliestSettlement: The Khmer Empire, centered at Angkor, dominated Southeast Asia from the 9th-15th centuries, building the vast temple complex of Angkor Wat.

keyDates.event: Khmer Empire founded, capital established at Angkor
Construction of Angkor Wat begins under Suryavarman II
Siamese forces sack Angkor, and the capital later moves south
Cambodia becomes a French protectorate
Independence from France
Lon Nol ousts Prince Sihanouk in a coup, proclaims the Khmer Republic
Khmer Rouge seizes power, begins genocide killing roughly 1.5-2 million people
Vietnamese forces oust the Khmer Rouge from power
Paris Peace Accords end decades of conflict
UN-supervised elections restore a constitutional monarchy under King Sihanouk

kh.climate: Tropical monsoon, hot and humid with a wet and dry season.
funFacts: Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world by land area.
The Khmer Rouge regime (1975-1979) killed an estimated quarter of Cambodia's population in one of the 20th century's worst genocides.
Cambodia's flag is one of the only national flags in the world to feature a building - Angkor Wat.
The Khmer Empire, which built Angkor Wat, was one of the most powerful civilizations in Southeast Asia, ruling from the 9th to 15th centuries.
Angkor is believed to have been the largest pre-industrial city in the world at its peak.
The Mekong River flows through Cambodia and feeds the Tonle Sap, Southeast Asia's largest freshwater lake.
Tonle Sap's flow actually reverses direction twice a year with the seasonal monsoon rains, a rare hydrological phenomenon.
Cambodia's traditional Apsara dance is inspired by celestial dancers depicted in ancient Khmer temple carvings.
Cambodia gained independence from France in 1953.
Phnom Penh, Cambodia's capital, sits at the confluence of the Mekong, Tonle Sap, and Bassac rivers.
kh.currencyNote: Cambodia's economy is substantially dollarized, with the US dollar circulating alongside the riel for most transactions.

la.earliestSettlement: The Kingdom of Lan Xang ('Million Elephants'), founded in 1353, was one of the largest states in Southeast Asian history, centered on the Mekong River.

keyDates.event: Kingdom of Lan Xang founded by Fa Ngum
Lan Xang splits into the rival kingdoms of Luang Prabang, Vientiane, and Champasak
Siam (Thailand) conquers and subjugates the Lao kingdoms
Laos becomes a French protectorate
Full independence from France
Laos becomes heavily bombed during the Vietnam War-era Secret War
Communist Pathet Lao takes power, monarchy abolished
Laos launches the 'New Economic Mechanism', market-oriented reforms
Laos joins ASEAN

la.climate: Tropical monsoon, hot and humid with a wet and dry season.
la.nationalSport: Petanque (brought by the French, hugely popular); football also widely followed

unesco.name: Vat Phou and Associated Ancient Settlements

funFacts: Laos is the most heavily bombed country per capita in history, from the US 'Secret War' during the Vietnam War era.
Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia.
The mysterious Plain of Jars features thousands of massive stone jars dating back over 2,000 years, whose purpose remains debated.
Luang Prabang, a former royal capital, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its many Buddhist temples and traditional architecture.
Laos gained independence from France in 1953 and became a communist state in 1975 after a long civil conflict.
The Mekong River runs the length of Laos and is central to transportation, fishing, and agriculture.
It is common to see saffron-robed Buddhist monks collecting morning alms in towns like Luang Prabang.
Laos is one of the few remaining single-party communist states in the world.
Sticky rice, traditionally eaten with the hands, is a dietary staple and a symbol of Lao identity.

bn.earliestSettlement: The Bruneian Empire, at its height in the 15th-16th centuries, controlled much of Borneo and the Philippines; the Sultanate has ruled continuously for over 600 years.

keyDates.event: Sultanate of Brunei founded
Reign of Sultan Bolkiah begins, Brunei's golden age as a regional power over Borneo and the Philippines
Brunei at the height of its regional power, visited by Magellan's expedition
Brunei cedes Sarawak to James Brooke, who becomes its Rajah
Brunei becomes a British protectorate
British Resident system introduced, giving Britain control over internal administration
Oil discovered, transforming the sultanate's economy
Brunei Revolt breaks out and is suppressed with British help
Full independence from Britain

bn.climate: Tropical rainforest, hot and humid year-round.
funFacts: Brunei's current sultan, Hassanal Bolkiah, has ruled continuously since 1967, one of the world's longest-reigning monarchs.
Brunei's oil and gas wealth gives it one of the highest GDP per capita figures in Asia, with no personal income tax.
The Sultanate of Brunei once controlled most of the island of Borneo and parts of the Philippines at its 16th-century peak.
Brunei sits on the island of Borneo, which it shares with Malaysia and Indonesia.
Brunei introduced Sharia-based criminal law provisions in stages starting in 2014, drawing international attention.
Kampong Ayer, a traditional stilt settlement on the Brunei River in the capital, is one of the largest water villages in the world, home to tens of thousands of people.
The Sultan's official residence, Istana Nurul Iman, is one of the largest residential palaces in the world.
Brunei's full official name is Negara Brunei Darussalam, meaning 'Abode of Peace'.
Brunei became fully independent from the United Kingdom in 1984, one of the last Southeast Asian nations to do so.
bn.currencyNote: The Brunei dollar is pegged 1:1 to and freely interchangeable with the Singapore dollar under a long-standing currency interchangeability agreement.

bt.independence: Never formally colonized; British influence over foreign affairs ended with a 1949 treaty
formerNames: Druk Yul (native name, 'Land of the Thunder Dragon')
bt.earliestSettlement: Buddhist culture has shaped Bhutan since the 7th-9th centuries; the country was unified as a nation-state by Ngawang Namgyal in the 17th century.

keyDates.event: Guru Rinpoche introduces Buddhism to Bhutan (traditional date)
Ngawang Namgyal unifies Bhutan and establishes the dual system of governance
Duar War with British India ends with the Treaty of Sinchula
Wangchuck dynasty founded, hereditary monarchy begins
Treaty of friendship signed with newly independent India
Bhutan joins the United Nations
Television and the internet introduced, among the last countries to do so
King Jigme Singye Wangchuck abdicates in favor of his son, paving the way for democracy
Bhutan transitions to a constitutional democracy

highestPeak.name: Gangkhar Puensum (unclimbed, one of the highest unclimbed mountains in the world)

bt.climate: Highly varied by altitude - subtropical lowlands to alpine high Himalaya.
funFacts: Bhutan famously measures national progress through Gross National Happiness rather than GDP alone.
Gangkhar Puensum, Bhutan's highest peak, is one of the highest mountains in the world never to have been climbed, as mountaineering above a certain altitude is banned for religious reasons.
Bhutan is one of the only carbon-negative countries in the world, absorbing more carbon than it emits.
Bhutan only allowed television and the internet in 1999, one of the last countries in the world to do so.
Bhutan was the first country in the world to ban the sale of tobacco, a law introduced in 2004.
Archery is Bhutan's national sport and is central to its festivals and village life.
Bhutan charges visiting tourists a daily sustainable development fee as part of a 'high-value, low-impact' tourism policy.
The Tiger's Nest monastery (Paro Taktsang) clings to a cliff face roughly 900 meters above the Paro valley.
Bhutan became a constitutional monarchy in 2008 when the king voluntarily ceded many of his powers.
Bhutan's flag features a dragon, or Druk, giving the country its native name, Druk Yul, 'Land of the Thunder Dragon'.
bt.currencyNote: Bhutan's ngultrum is pegged 1:1 to the Indian rupee, and Indian rupees are also accepted as legal tender in the country.
bt.territorialNote: Bhutan and China have an unresolved border dispute in the Himalayas, including the Doklam plateau, an area also of strategic concern to India.

mv.earliestSettlement: Settled by seafaring peoples from South Asia over 2,500 years ago; converted from Buddhism to Islam in 1153, a defining event still central to national identity.

keyDates.event: Conversion to Islam under Sultan Muhammad ibn Abdullah
Portuguese briefly occupy Male
Becomes a British protectorate
First written constitution adopted
Independence from Britain
Sultanate abolished, republic established
Indian Ocean tsunami devastates the islands
New democratic constitution adopted; first multi-party presidential election won by Mohamed Nasheed

highestPeak.name: Unnamed point on Villingili Island, Addu Atoll (lowest-lying country in the world)

mv.climate: Tropical, hot and humid year-round with a monsoon season.
mv.nationalAnimal: Skipjack tuna (central to the economy and cuisine)
majorReligions: Islam (official and sole legally permitted religion)
funFacts: The Maldives is the lowest-lying country in the world, with an average elevation of just about 1.5 meters above sea level.
The Maldives is made up of around 1,192 coral islands grouped into 26 atolls.
Rising sea levels pose an existential threat to the Maldives, prompting the government to explore relocation options for its population.
The Maldives has no rivers; its flat, low-lying islands are too small to support them.
Male, the capital, is one of the most densely populated cities in the world relative to its tiny land area.
The Maldives became a republic in 1968, ending a long-running sultanate that had lasted for centuries.
Cowrie shells harvested in the Maldives were once traded as currency across parts of Asia and East Africa.
Tourism, which began in the 1970s, is now the backbone of the Maldivian economy, with many resorts built on their own private islands.
Maldivian cuisine relies heavily on fish, especially skipjack tuna, alongside coconut and starchy staples like breadfruit.

formerNames: Territory of Papua and New Guinea
pg.earliestSettlement: Human settlement dates back at least 40,000-60,000 years, with highland peoples independently developing agriculture among the earliest in the world, around 7,000-10,000 years ago.

keyDates.event: Independent development of agriculture in the New Guinea Highlands (approx.)
Portuguese explorer Jorge de Menezes becomes among the first Europeans to sight New Guinea
Germany and Britain divide the eastern half of New Guinea between them
British New Guinea transferred to Australia as the Territory of Papua
Australia receives a mandate over former German New Guinea after WWI
Fierce WWII Pacific campaign fighting (e.g. Kokoda Track) takes place
First House of Assembly elections, early steps toward self-government
Independence from Australia
Bougainville conflict begins (ends 1998)

pg.climate: Tropical, hot and humid year-round with a wet and dry season.
funFacts: Papua New Guinea is one of the most linguistically diverse countries on Earth, with over 800 living languages.
The Kuk Early Agricultural Site shows evidence of independent agricultural development nearly 10,000 years ago, among the earliest in the world.
Papua New Guinea shares its island with Indonesia, one of the few places in the world where a single island is divided between two very different countries.
Papua New Guinea is home to hundreds of distinct tribal groups, each with its own customs and language.
The bird-of-paradise, famed for its elaborate plumage, is a national symbol of Papua New Guinea and appears on its flag.
Port Moresby, the capital, has no road connection to most of the rest of the country because of the rugged mountainous terrain.
Papua New Guinea gained independence from Australia in 1975.
The Kokoda Track, a wartime trail across the Owen Stanley Range, was the site of fierce fighting between Australian and Japanese forces in World War II.
pg.territorialNote: Bougainville, an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea, voted overwhelmingly for independence in a 2019 referendum, though full independence has not yet been implemented.

fj.earliestSettlement: Settled by Austronesian and Melanesian voyagers roughly 3,500 years ago; became a British crown colony in 1874 after a period of unification under local chiefs.

keyDates.event: Earliest Lapita settlers arrive in Fiji (approx.)
Dutch explorer Abel Tasman becomes first European to sight Fiji
Fiji becomes a British crown colony
Indian indentured laborers begin arriving to work sugar plantations
Independence from Britain
First of several military coups
Military coup led by Frank Bainimarama
Return to parliamentary democracy after the 2006 coup

fj.climate: Tropical maritime, warm year-round with a wet and dry season.
funFacts: Fiji won its first Olympic medal ever - a gold - in rugby sevens at the 2016 Rio Games.
Fiji sits near the International Date Line, among the first places on Earth to see each new day.
Fiji is home to a significant population of Indo-Fijians, descendants of indentured laborers brought by the British in the late 19th century.
Fiji is made up of more than 330 islands, roughly a third of which are inhabited.
'Bula', meaning 'life' or 'hello', is Fiji's famously warm and widely used greeting.
Kava, a traditional drink made from a native plant's root, plays a central role in Fijian ceremonies and social life.
The Great Astrolabe Reef off Kadavu Island is one of the largest barrier reefs in the world.
Fiji was a major producer of sugar cane during the British colonial era, which shaped much of its modern demographics.

sb.earliestSettlement: Settled by Papuan-speaking peoples thousands of years ago, with later Austronesian migration; named by Spanish explorer Alvaro de Mendana in 1568.

keyDates.event: Spanish explorer Alvaro de Mendana names the islands
Britain declares a protectorate over the southern Solomons
Battle of Guadalcanal, a major turning point of WWII in the Pacific
Independence from Britain
Ethnic tensions begin (ends 2003 with regional intervention)
Regional Assistance Mission to Solomon Islands (RAMSI) concludes

sb.climate: Tropical rainforest, hot and humid year-round.
funFacts: The Battle of Guadalcanal (1942-43), fought in the Solomon Islands, was one of the most pivotal campaigns of WWII in the Pacific.
The Solomon Islands consist of nearly 1,000 islands spread across a vast ocean area.
The islands were named 'Solomon' by a Spanish explorer who mistakenly believed he had found the biblical King Solomon's gold mines.
The Solomon Islands gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1978.
The islands lie on the Pacific 'Ring of Fire,' with active volcanoes and frequent earthquakes.
The Solomon Islands has extraordinary linguistic diversity, with more than 70 distinct languages spoken among its small population.
Traditional shell money is still used in parts of the Solomon Islands for ceremonial exchanges such as dowries.
The waters around the Solomon Islands sit within the Coral Triangle, one of the world's richest zones of coral reef biodiversity.

vu.independence: July 30, 1980, from France and the United Kingdom (jointly, the unusual Anglo-French Condominium)
vu.earliestSettlement: Settled by Austronesian peoples roughly 3,000 years ago; named the New Hebrides by Captain Cook in 1774 and later jointly administered by Britain and France.

keyDates.event: Portuguese explorer Pedro Fernandes de Queiros becomes the first European to sight the islands
Captain James Cook names the islands the New Hebrides
Britain and France establish a joint Anglo-French Condominium
Independence as Vanuatu, ending the unique dual-colonial arrangement
Cyclone Pam devastates the country

vu.climate: Tropical, warm and humid with a cyclone season.
funFacts: Vanuatu was governed under a unique joint British-French 'condominium,' a rare arrangement of two colonial powers ruling the same territory simultaneously.
Mount Yasur, one of the world's most accessible active volcanoes, has been erupting continuously for hundreds of years.
Vanuatu is famous for its traditional land diving ritual on Pentecost Island, a precursor to modern bungee jumping.
Vanuatu comprises more than 80 islands stretching across the South Pacific.
Vanuatu is regularly ranked among the happiest and most ecologically sustainable countries in the world in the Happy Planet Index.
The country was known as the New Hebrides before gaining independence in 1980.
Vanuatu is highly exposed to natural disasters, including cyclones, volcanic eruptions and earthquakes.
Bislama, an English-based creole, is one of Vanuatu's official languages alongside English and French.

government.form: Unitary parliamentary republic (with a traditional O le Ao o le Malo head of state)

ws.independence: January 1, 1962, from New Zealand (first Pacific island nation to gain independence in the 20th century)
ws.earliestSettlement: Settled by Austronesian voyagers around 3,000 years ago; Samoa is considered one of the cradles of Polynesian culture, with its traditional fa'a Samoa way of life still central today.

keyDates.event: Early Polynesian settlement and culture develop in Samoa (approx.)
London Missionary Society introduces Christianity to Samoa
Samoa divided between Germany (west) and the US (east, American Samoa)
New Zealand occupies German Samoa during WWI
Independence from New Zealand - first Pacific nation to do so in the modern era
Country officially renamed from Western Samoa to Samoa

ws.climate: Tropical, warm and humid year-round with a wet and dry season.
funFacts: Samoa was the first Pacific island nation to gain independence in the 20th century, in 1962.
In 2011, Samoa skipped December 30 entirely, moving to the other side of the International Date Line to better align with its trading partners Australia and New Zealand.
Samoa's traditional fa'a Samoa ('the Samoan way') social and chiefly system remains central to daily life and governance.
Samoa consists of two main islands, Upolu and Savai'i, along with several smaller islands.
Author Robert Louis Stevenson, who wrote 'Treasure Island,' lived in Samoa for the last years of his life and is buried there.
Rugby union is hugely popular in Samoa, and the national team, Manu Samoa, has sent many players on to top international clubs.
Samoa switched from driving on the right side of the road to the left in 2009, to align with Australia and New Zealand.

to.independence: June 4, 1970, from the United Kingdom (Tonga was never formally colonized, but was a British-protected state)
formerNames: Friendly Islands (name given by Captain Cook)
to.earliestSettlement: Settled by Austronesian voyagers around 3,000 years ago; the Tu'i Tonga Empire, from around the 10th century, was one of the most powerful and far-reaching Polynesian states in history.

keyDates.event: Tu'i Tonga Empire founded, rises to regional dominance (approx.)
Captain Cook visits and nicknames Tonga 'the Friendly Islands'
King George Tupou I unifies Tonga and begins modernization
Tonga's first constitution adopted, establishing a constitutional monarchy
Tonga becomes a British-protected state (retaining internal self-rule)
Full independence from Britain
Massive Hunga Tonga volcanic eruption, one of the largest in recorded history

to.climate: Tropical, warm and humid with a cyclone season.
to.nationalAnimal: Flying fox (fruit bat, protected as a royal symbol)
funFacts: Tonga is the only Pacific island nation never formally colonized by a foreign power.
The 2022 Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai eruption was one of the most powerful volcanic events ever recorded by modern instruments.
Tonga's monarchy traces its line back over a thousand years, among the oldest continuous monarchies in the world.
Tonga consists of 169 islands, only 36 of which are inhabited.
Tonga switched from driving on the right to driving on the left in the 1970s, to match its Pacific neighbors.
Tongan-born and Tongan-descended players have had an outsized influence on international rugby, starring for teams such as New Zealand, Australia, and Japan.
Tonga lies just west of the International Date Line, making it one of the first places on Earth to welcome each new day.
The umu, a traditional underground earth oven, is central to Tongan feasts and is shared across much of Polynesia.

ki.earliestSettlement: Settled by Micronesian and later Polynesian voyagers around 3,000 years ago, spread across a vast area of the central Pacific.

keyDates.event: British navigators sight the Gilbert Islands
Britain establishes the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Protectorate
Gilbert and Ellice Islands become a British colony
Battle of Tarawa, one of the bloodiest Pacific battles of WWII
Ellice Islands separate to become Tuvalu
Gilbert Islands gain independence as Kiribati
Kiribati purchases land in Fiji as a potential future refuge from rising seas
Kiribati switches diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China

ki.nationalSport: Te ano (traditional ball game); football also played
funFacts: Kiribati is the only country in the world situated in all four hemispheres (north, south, east and west).
Kiribati moved part of the International Date Line in 1995 so the entire country could share the same calendar day.
Kiribati is one of the countries most threatened by rising sea levels, with its highest point only around 81 meters above sea level.
Kiribati is made up of 33 atolls and reef islands spread across a vast area of the central Pacific Ocean.
Kiribati gained independence from Britain in 1979, when it was previously known as the Gilbert Islands.
Fishing and coconut-based products are central to Kiribati's traditional economy and diet.
Because of the shifted date line, Kiribati is among the first places on Earth to see each new day.
The capital, South Tarawa, is one of the most densely populated places on Earth relative to its tiny landmass.

tv.earliestSettlement: Settled by Polynesian voyagers many centuries ago; administered jointly with the Gilbert Islands until separating in 1975-1978.

keyDates.event: Britain establishes the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Protectorate
Ellice Islands vote to separate from the Gilbert Islands
Independence as Tuvalu
Tuvalu joins the United Nations
Tuvalu leases its '.tv' internet domain, a major source of national revenue
Tuvalu announces plans to create a 'digital nation' in the metaverse in case of submersion

funFacts: Tuvalu is one of the smallest and least populous sovereign states in the world, with only around 11,000 people.
Tuvalu earns significant national revenue by licensing its '.tv' internet domain to streaming and media companies worldwide.
Tuvalu's highest point is less than 5 meters above sea level, making it one of the countries most vulnerable to climate change.
Tuvalu has no standing armed forces, relying instead on a small police force for law enforcement and maritime surveillance.
Tuvalu became the 189th member of the United Nations in the year 2000.
Funafuti, the capital atoll, is a narrow strip of land surrounding a lagoon, and its airstrip doubles as a community gathering space outside flight hours.
Tuvalu has become a prominent international voice on climate change, including proposing a 'digital nation' project to preserve its government and culture online.
Tuvalu was formerly known as the Ellice Islands under British colonial rule before adopting its current name upon independence in 1978.

nr.independence: January 31, 1968, from Australia, New Zealand and the UK (jointly, as a UN trust territory)
nr.earliestSettlement: Settled by Micronesian and Polynesian peoples around 3,000 years ago; became fabulously wealthy in the 20th century from extensive phosphate mining.

keyDates.event: Germany annexes Nauru
Phosphate mining begins, eventually making Nauru one of the richest countries per capita
Australian forces occupy Nauru during WWI
Japanese occupation during WWII
Independence
Phosphate reserves begin to be significantly depleted
Nauru begins hosting Australian offshore asylum-seeker processing

nr.nationalSport: Australian rules football (uniquely popular for a non-Australian nation); weightlifting also notable
funFacts: Nauru is the smallest island nation in the world and the third-smallest country overall by area.
Once among the richest countries per capita due to phosphate mining, Nauru's economy collapsed as reserves ran out, leaving much of the island environmentally devastated.
Nauru has no official capital city - government functions are centered in the Yaren district.
Early European explorers nicknamed Nauru 'Pleasant Island' for its lush appearance before phosphate mining scarred its interior.
At one point Nauru operated its own national airline, Air Nauru, an unusually large undertaking for such a tiny country.
Nauru receives very few international visitors each year, making it one of the least-visited countries in the world.
Nauru has switched diplomatic recognition between Taiwan and China more than once, reflecting how even tiny states can carry outsized geopolitical weight.
Nauruan, spoken only on the island, is one of the smallest language communities in the Pacific.
nr.currencyNote: Nauru has no currency of its own and uses the Australian dollar.

government.form: Unitary presidential republic (in free association with the United States)

pw.independence: October 1, 1994, from the United States (UN trusteeship, under a Compact of Free Association)
formerNames: Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands (as part of)
pw.earliestSettlement: Settled by seafaring peoples from Southeast Asia roughly 3,000 years ago, developing one of the most distinctive traditional societies in Micronesia.

keyDates.event: Spain claims Palau as part of the Spanish East Indies
Spain sells Palau to Germany as part of the Caroline Islands
Japan occupies Palau after WWI, administers it as a League of Nations mandate
Battle of Peleliu, one of the fiercest WWII Pacific battles, fought in Palau
Palau becomes part of the US-administered Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands
Independence under a Compact of Free Association with the US

pw.nationalAnimal: Fruit bat (dugong also a protected symbol)

nationalDish.name: Fruit bat soup (traditional; tapioca and fish also staples)

funFacts: Palau created the world's first shark sanctuary, banning commercial shark fishing across its entire exclusive economic zone.
Palau requires every visitor to sign a 'Palau Pledge' in their passport, a legally binding environmental commitment to protect the islands.
The Rock Islands' Jellyfish Lake is home to millions of jellyfish that have evolved to lose most of their sting due to the absence of natural predators.
Palau was among the last places on Earth to be permanently settled by people, with habitation dating back around 3,000 years.
Palau's Rock Islands are hundreds of mushroom-shaped limestone islets, carved into their distinctive shape by erosion at the waterline.
Palau uses the US dollar as its currency, reflecting its close relationship with the United States under a Compact of Free Association.
Palau has no standing military and relies on the United States for its defense under that Compact.
The Rock Islands Southern Lagoon is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, valued for both its marine biodiversity and ancient rock art.
With a population of roughly 18,000, Palau is one of the smallest nations in the world by population.
pw.currencyNote: Palau has no currency of its own and uses the US dollar as its official legal tender.

az.independence: May 28, 1918 (first republic, briefly); August 30, 1991, from the Soviet Union
az.earliestSettlement: A historic crossroads on the Silk Road, home to ancient civilizations including the kingdom of Caucasian Albania (unrelated to modern Albania); strongly shaped by Persian, Turkic and Russian influence over centuries.

keyDates.event: Kingdom of Caucasian Albania emerges as an ancient state in the region (approx.)
Arab conquest brings Islam to the region (approx.)
Safavid dynasty established under Shah Ismail I, with Azerbaijan as a core region
Treaty of Turkmenchay divides Azerbaijan between the Russian and Persian empires
Azerbaijan Democratic Republic declared, first secular democratic republic in the Muslim world
Soviet Red Army invades, ending the first republic
Nagorno-Karabakh conflict with Armenia begins
Independence from the Soviet Union
Bishkek Protocol ceasefire ends the First Nagorno-Karabakh War
Second Nagorno-Karabakh War, Azerbaijan regains significant territory

az.climate: Highly varied - subtropical on the Caspian coast, semi-arid steppe, alpine in the Caucasus mountains.
az.nationalSport: Chovgan (traditional horseback game); football most popular
funFacts: Azerbaijan's capital Baku sits below sea level, one of the lowest-lying capital cities in the world.
The 1918 Azerbaijan Democratic Republic was the first secular parliamentary republic in the Muslim world and the first in the world to grant women full voting rights on equal terms.
Azerbaijan is home to mud volcanoes, a rare geological phenomenon found in concentrated numbers nowhere else on Earth.
Azerbaijan is often called the 'Land of Fire' for its ancient natural gas vents, which fueled a long tradition of Zoroastrian fire worship.
Baku's Flame Towers, completed in 2012, have become the defining symbol of the modern city skyline.
The walled Old City (Icherisheher) of Baku, with roots on the ancient Silk Road, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Azerbaijan hosted the inaugural European Games in Baku in 2015.
Azerbaijan's territory spans an unusually wide range of climate zones for its size, from subtropical lowlands to alpine mountains.
az.territorialNote: Azerbaijan and Armenia have long disputed the Nagorno-Karabakh region, with Azerbaijan regaining control of most of the territory following conflicts in 2020 and 2023.

am.earliestSettlement: Armenia is one of the oldest continuous civilizations, with the Kingdom of Urartu flourishing around the 9th century BC; Armenia became the first nation in the world to adopt Christianity as a state religion in 301 AD.

keyDates.event: Kingdom of Urartu emerges as a major power centered on Lake Van (approx.)
Tigranes the Great expands the Armenian Empire to its greatest extent
Armenia becomes the first country to adopt Christianity as its state religion
Mesrop Mashtots invents the unique Armenian alphabet
Armenian kingdom dissolved, divided between Byzantine and Persian empires
Bagratid Armenian kingdom restored
Byzantine conquest ends the Bagratid kingdom
Fall of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, the last Armenian state until the modern era
Armenian Genocide under the Ottoman Empire kills over a million Armenians
First Republic of Armenia declared
Sovietized, becoming part of the USSR
First Nagorno-Karabakh War with Azerbaijan begins
Independence from the Soviet Union
Second Nagorno-Karabakh War results in significant territorial losses

famousFeature.name: Lake Sevan / Mount Ararat (visible from Armenia, located in Turkey)

am.climate: Highland continental, hot dry summers and cold snowy winters.
am.nationalAnimal: Eagle (golden eagle, depicted on the coat of arms)
am.nationalSport: Chess (officially part of the school curriculum, nationally significant); wrestling and weightlifting strong internationally
funFacts: Armenia became the first nation in the world to adopt Christianity as a state religion, in 301 AD.
Armenia has a unique 39-letter alphabet, invented specifically for the language in 405 AD and still used today.
Yerevan is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, older than Rome.
Mount Ararat, the spiritual symbol of Armenia and the traditional resting place of Noah's Ark, actually lies within modern-day Turkey.
The Armenian Genocide of 1915-1923, in which an estimated 1.5 million Armenians were killed by the Ottoman Empire, is commemorated every April 24.
Lake Sevan is one of the largest high-altitude freshwater lakes in the world.
Chess has been a mandatory school subject in Armenia since 2011, reflecting the country's strong chess culture.
The Areni-1 cave complex in Armenia contains the world's oldest known winery, dating back roughly 6,100 years.
Armenian khachkars — intricately carved memorial cross-stones — are a unique art form recognized by UNESCO.
am.territorialNote: Armenia and Azerbaijan have long disputed the Nagorno-Karabakh region, with Azerbaijan regaining control of most of the territory following conflicts in 2020 and 2023.

ge.independence: May 26, 1918 (first republic, briefly); April 9, 1991, from the Soviet Union
ge.earliestSettlement: One of the earliest centers of wine production in the world, with evidence of winemaking dating back 8,000 years; the medieval Kingdom of Georgia reached its golden age under Queen Tamar in the 12th-13th centuries.

keyDates.event: Traditional founding of the Kingdom of Iberia in eastern Georgia
Kingdom of Iberia (eastern Georgia) adopts Christianity

ge.climate: Varied - subtropical on the Black Sea coast, alpine in the Caucasus, continental inland.
ge.nationalSport: Rugby union; wrestling and judo also strong internationally
funFacts: Georgia is widely considered the birthplace of wine, with archaeological evidence of winemaking dating back roughly 8,000 years.
The Georgian language has its own unique alphabet, unrelated to Latin, Cyrillic or Greek scripts.
Soviet leader Joseph Stalin was born in Gori, Georgia.
Georgia sits at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, with the Caucasus Mountains forming much of its northern border.
The ancient kingdom of Colchis, on Georgia's Black Sea coast, is linked in Greek mythology to the legend of Jason and the Golden Fleece.
Georgian cuisine is famous worldwide for khachapuri, a cheese-filled bread, and khinkali, a type of filled dumpling.
Tbilisi, the capital, is known for the sulfur bath houses of its historic old town.
Georgian polyphonic singing, a distinctive multi-part vocal tradition, is recognized by UNESCO as part of humanity's Intangible Cultural Heritage.
Georgia declared independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
ge.territorialNote: The breakaway regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia are administered as de facto independent territories with Russian support but are recognized internationally as part of Georgia.

pa.earliestSettlement: Indigenous peoples inhabited the isthmus for thousands of years; became a key Spanish colonial transit point for gold and silver shipped from Peru, due to its narrow land bridge between the oceans.

pa.climate: Tropical, hot and humid year-round with a wet and dry season.

unesco.name: Fortifications on the Caribbean Side of Panama

funFacts: The Panama Canal, a feat of early 20th-century engineering, cuts the sea voyage between the Atlantic and Pacific by thousands of miles.
Panama is one of the few places in the world where you can see the sun rise over the Pacific and set over the Atlantic, due to the canal's unusual east-west orientation.
Panama is a major hub for international banking and shipping, with one of the world's largest ship registries.
Panama uses the US dollar alongside its own currency, the balboa, which is pegged 1:1 to the dollar.
Panama City is one of the only capital cities in the world with a tropical rainforest reserve inside its city limits.
Panama separated from Colombia in 1903, shortly before agreeing to let the United States build the Panama Canal.
The Darien Gap, a roadless stretch of jungle on the Panama-Colombia border, is one of the few breaks in the Pan-American Highway.
Panama hats actually originated in Ecuador, but became associated with Panama after workers wore them while building the canal.
topExports: re-exported goods via the Colón Free Zone
pa.currencyNote: Panama uses the US dollar as its primary circulating currency alongside its own balboa, which exists mainly as coinage.

cr.earliestSettlement: Indigenous peoples inhabited the region for millennia before Spanish arrival; developed differently from neighboring colonies due to a lack of major mineral wealth, fostering a more egalitarian smallholder society.

cr.climate: Tropical, varying with altitude; a distinct wet and dry season.

unesco.name: Precolumbian Chiefdom Settlements with Stone Spheres

funFacts: Costa Rica abolished its military entirely in 1948, redirecting funds toward education and healthcare.
Costa Rica generates nearly all of its electricity from renewable sources and is widely regarded as a global leader in conservation and ecotourism.
Despite covering just 0.03% of the Earth's surface, Costa Rica is home to about 5% of the world's biodiversity.
'Pura vida', meaning 'pure life', is Costa Rica's unofficial national motto and everyday greeting.
Costa Rica's cloud forests, such as Monteverde, host extraordinary biodiversity, including the resplendent quetzal.
Costa Rica regularly ranks among the happiest countries in the world in global happiness surveys.
Costa Rica has been a pioneer of sustainable ecotourism since the 1980s, long before it became a global trend.
Costa Rica's name means 'rich coast' in Spanish, reportedly given by early Spanish explorers.

gt.earliestSettlement: The heartland of the ancient Maya civilization, with great cities like Tikal flourishing from around 600 BC to 900 AD before mysterious decline.

majorReligions: Christianity (Roman Catholic and growing Protestant share)
funFacts: Guatemala is home to Tikal, one of the largest and most important Maya archaeological sites, with pyramids rising over 60 meters.
Guatemala's currency, the quetzal, is named after the resplendent quetzal, a bird considered sacred by the ancient Maya.
Guatemala has the largest population of any Central American country.
More than 20 Mayan languages are still spoken in Guatemala today, alongside Spanish.
Lake Atitlan, ringed by volcanoes, is often cited as one of the most beautiful lakes in the world.
Guatemala is one of the world's top producers of cardamom, a spice widely used in Middle Eastern and South Asian cooking.
Antigua Guatemala, a former colonial capital, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its well-preserved Spanish Baroque architecture.
Guatemala has 37 volcanoes, including several, like Volcan de Fuego, that remain active.
The ancient Maya consumed cacao as a ceremonial drink, giving Guatemala deep historical roots in the story of chocolate.

funFacts: Copan was one of the most important centers of astronomy and hieroglyphic writing in the ancient Maya world.
Honduras gave the English language the term 'banana republic,' coined to describe the country's early 20th-century dependence on American fruit companies.
The Bay Islands off Honduras, including Roatan, sit on the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, the second-largest coral reef system in the world.
Spanish is the official language of Honduras, though Garifuna and several indigenous languages are also spoken.
The Lenca, an indigenous people of western Honduras, have a long history of resistance and cultural continuity.
Tegucigalpa, the capital, takes its unusual name from an indigenous word thought to mean 'silver hill.'
Honduras is one of the most biodiverse countries in Central America, home to jaguars, toucans, and hundreds of orchid species.
Honduras is thought to take its name from the Spanish word for 'depths,' reportedly a reference to deep coastal waters noted by early Spanish explorers.

sv.earliestSettlement: Home to Maya and later Pipil (Nahua) peoples before Spanish conquest in the 1520s; the smallest and most densely populated country in mainland Central America.

sv.climate: Tropical, with a pronounced wet and dry season.
majorReligions: Christianity (Roman Catholic and growing Protestant share)
funFacts: El Salvador became the first country in the world to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender, in 2021.
El Salvador is the smallest and most densely populated country in mainland Central America.

A sweeping security crackdown beginning in 2022 dramatically cut El Salvador's homicide rate, transforming it from one of the world's most violent countries by some measures, though drawing significant human-rights criticism.
El Salvador is nicknamed the 'Land of Volcanoes,' with around 20 volcanoes dotting its landscape.
Pupusas, thick corn tortillas stuffed with cheese, beans, or meat, are considered the national dish of El Salvador.
The ancient Maya village of Joya de Cerén, buried by a volcanic eruption around 600 AD, is so well preserved it is sometimes called the 'Pompeii of the Americas.'
El Salvador is the only Central American country without a coastline on the Caribbean Sea, bordering only the Pacific Ocean.
Surfing is hugely popular in El Salvador, and Pacific beaches such as El Tunco are internationally known surf destinations.
sv.currencyNote: El Salvador fully dollarized its economy in 2001, adopting the US dollar as official currency in place of the Salvadoran colón.

ni.climate: Tropical, with a pronounced wet and dry season.
majorReligions: Christianity (Roman Catholic and growing Protestant share)
funFacts: Nicaragua is the largest country in Central America by land area.
Lake Nicaragua is one of the only freshwater lakes in the world known to have historically supported bull sharks.
Nicaragua gave the world the renowned poet Ruben Dario, a founding figure of the Spanish-language literary movement known as modernismo.
Nicaragua is home to two of the largest lakes in Central America, Lake Nicaragua and Lake Managua.
Nicaragua has nearly 20 volcanoes, several still active, earning it the nickname 'Land of Lakes and Volcanoes.'
In the 19th century, Nicaragua was seriously considered as the site for an interoceanic canal, decades before Panama was ultimately chosen.
Ometepe Island, formed by two volcanoes rising from Lake Nicaragua, is the largest island located within a freshwater lake in the world.
Nicaragua gained independence from Spain in 1821 as part of the short-lived Federal Republic of Central America.
ni.currencyNote: Nicaragua suffered severe hyperinflation in the late 1980s, leading to the introduction of a new córdoba currency in 1991.
ni.territorialNote: Nicaragua and Colombia have a long-running maritime and territorial dispute over islands and waters in the Caribbean Sea, addressed in several international court rulings.

funFacts: North Korea remains one of the most isolated and tightly controlled societies in the world, with strict limits on information and travel.
The Korean War technically never formally ended - the 1953 armistice was a ceasefire, not a peace treaty, leaving the two Koreas technically still at war.
Pyongyang's unfinished 105-story Ryugyong Hotel has stood as a concrete shell since the early 1990s, a famous symbol of stalled ambition.
North Korea is officially known as the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
The country was established in 1948 after the Korean peninsula was divided following World War II.
North Korea uses its own calendar system, the Juche calendar, which counts years starting from the birth of founder Kim Il Sung in 1912.
The Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea is one of the most heavily fortified borders in the world.
kp.currencyNote: North Korea's 2009 currency redenomination wiped out much of the population's cash savings and caused significant economic disruption.
kp.territorialNote: North and South Korea have been divided by the Demilitarized Zone since the 1953 armistice, as no formal peace treaty was ever signed.

funFacts: Albania has more bunkers per capita than almost any country — about 175,000 concrete bunkers built under Hoxha's paranoid defense policy.
Albanians nod for 'no' and shake their head for 'yes', the reverse of most of the world.
Albania was one of the most isolated countries in the world under communist rule from 1944 to 1991, largely cut off from the outside world.
Gjirokastër and Berat, known as Albania's 'museum cities', are UNESCO World Heritage Sites prized for their Ottoman-era architecture.
The Albanian Riviera along the Ionian Sea has become an increasingly popular destination for its turquoise water and dramatic coastline.
Albania's flag features a black double-headed eagle, a symbol with roots in the Byzantine Empire and the 15th-century hero Skanderbeg.
Albania joined NATO in 2009 and is currently negotiating to join the European Union.
Tirana's main square once held a giant statue of communist dictator Enver Hoxha, which was torn down by crowds in 1991.
Albanian forms its own distinct branch of the Indo-European language family, not closely related to any neighboring language.

funFacts: Belarus is home to Europe's last remaining primeval lowland forest, Bialowieza, shared with Poland.
Belarus is a landlocked country with no direct access to the sea, bordering Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.
Belarusian and Russian are both official languages, though Russian dominates everyday life.
Minsk was almost completely destroyed during World War II and was rebuilt largely in Soviet architectural style.
The 1986 Chernobyl disaster, though centered in Ukraine, deposited the bulk of its radioactive fallout on Belarusian territory.
Belarus is nicknamed 'the lungs of Europe' for its extensive forests, marshes and wetlands.
Draniki, fried potato pancakes, are considered a national dish of Belarus.
Alexander Lukashenko has led Belarus since 1994, making him one of Europe's longest-serving heads of state.
by.currencyNote: Belarus redenominated its currency in 2016, removing four zeros to introduce a new Belarusian ruble.

The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in 1914 triggered the chain of events leading to World War I.
The Stari Most (Old Bridge) in Mostar, originally built in 1566, was destroyed during the 1990s war and rebuilt in 2004 using traditional methods.
Sutjeska National Park protects Perućica, one of the last primeval forests remaining in Europe.
Sarajevo is sometimes nicknamed the 'Jerusalem of Europe' for its historic mix of mosques, synagogues, and Catholic and Orthodox churches standing close together.
Bosnian coffee, brewed and served in a distinctive copper džezva pot, remains central to everyday social life.
The 1995 Dayton Agreement ended the Bosnian War and established the country's current structure of two entities under one state.
ba.currencyNote: Bosnia and Herzegovina's convertible mark operates under a currency board, pegged first to the German mark and now the euro, introduced in 1998 after the hyperinflation of the former Yugoslavia.

funFacts: Cyprus is the mythological birthplace of Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love, said to have emerged from the sea near Paphos.
Nicosia is the world's last divided capital city, split between the Republic of Cyprus and Turkish-controlled northern Cyprus since 1974.
Cyprus is the third largest and third most populous island in the Mediterranean Sea, after Sicily and Sardinia.
The country's name is linked to copper: the Latin word for copper, 'cuprum', is believed to derive from 'Cyprus', a major ancient source of the metal.
Halloumi, the squeaky grilling cheese that originated in Cyprus, was granted protected European Union status in 2021.
Commandaria, a sweet wine produced in Cyprus since antiquity, is often cited as the oldest named wine still in production today.
The United Nations has maintained a buffer zone, nicknamed the Green Line, across the island since 1974.
Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoic philosophy, was born in the Cypriot city of Kition, modern-day Larnaca.
Cyprus hosts two British Overseas Territory military bases, Akrotiri and Dhekelia, a legacy of British colonial rule.
Cyprus joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2008.
cy.territorialNote: The northern part of the island has been administered as the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus since 1974, recognized only by Turkey, while the Republic of Cyprus and most of the international community recognize Cypriot sovereignty over the whole island.

funFacts: Estonia is one of the most digitally advanced countries in the world — citizens can vote, file taxes, and even start a company entirely online, and the country invented Skype.
Estonia has over 2,000 islands, though only a small number are inhabited.
More than half of Estonia's land area is covered by forest.
Estonia offers 'e-Residency', a digital identity that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an EU-based business online.
Estonian is a Finno-Ugric language closely related to Finnish, and quite different from the Baltic languages of neighbouring Latvia and Lithuania.
Estonia's nationwide Song Festival, held roughly every five years, gathers tens of thousands of singers and was central to the peaceful 'Singing Revolution' that helped end Soviet rule in 1991.
Tallinn's Old Town is one of the best-preserved medieval city centres in Northern Europe.
Estonia has one of the highest numbers of tech startups per capita in Europe.

funFacts: Moldova is one of Europe's largest wine producers relative to its size, with wine cellars like Mileștii Mici holding the Guinness World Record for the largest wine collection, stretching over 200 km of underground tunnels.
Transnistria, a breakaway strip of Moldova, still uses Soviet-era symbols on its flag and is not recognized by any UN member state.
Moldova is one of the least visited countries in Europe, though its wine routes and monasteries are drawing growing tourist interest.
Moldova declared independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
Orheiul Vechi, a cave monastery complex carved into limestone cliffs, dates back over 2,000 years and remains an active religious site.
Moldova is landlocked but has a narrow stretch of access to the Danube River, giving it a small outlet toward the Black Sea.
Chișinău, Moldova's capital, was almost entirely rebuilt after suffering massive destruction in World War II.
Romanian is the official language of Moldova, and the two countries share deep cultural and historical ties.
md.territorialNote: Moldova's Transnistria region functions as a self-declared, internationally unrecognized de facto state with its own government and currency, following a 1992 conflict.

funFacts: Montenegro's name literally means 'Black Mountain', referring to the dark, densely forested peaks of Mount Lovćen.
The Bay of Kotor is often called Europe's southernmost fjord, though geologically it's a submerged river canyon.
Montenegro gained independence from its union with Serbia through a 2006 referendum.
Durmitor National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is home to the Tara River Canyon, the deepest canyon in Europe.
Montenegro uses the euro as its de facto currency without being an official member of the eurozone.
Cetinje served as Montenegro's historic royal capital and remains its ceremonial 'old royal capital' today.
Montenegro is one of the most mountainous countries in Europe, a landscape reflected directly in its name.
me.currencyNote: Montenegro unilaterally adopted the German mark and later the euro as its official currency without being a member of the eurozone or EU.

funFacts: Lake Ohrid is one of the oldest lakes in the world, estimated at 1.4 to 2 million years old, and home to unique endemic species.
North Macedonia got its current name only in 2019 after a 27-year naming dispute with Greece over the historical region of Macedonia.
North Macedonia is a landlocked Balkan country that was part of Yugoslavia until declaring independence in 1991.
The country joined NATO in 2020 after resolving its naming dispute with Greece through the Prespa Agreement.
Skopje, the capital, was largely rebuilt after a devastating 1963 earthquake that destroyed much of the city.
The Tikveš wine region has been producing wine since antiquity and remains North Macedonia's largest wine-growing area today.
The ancient kingdom of Macedon, associated with Alexander the Great, covered parts of this region, a historical link central to the country's identity.

funFacts: Malta's Ġgantija temples predate Stonehenge and the Egyptian pyramids, making them among the oldest free-standing structures on Earth.
Malta is one of the smallest and most densely populated countries in the world, roughly a third the size of New York City.
Malta was a British colony until gaining independence in 1964, and English remains an official language alongside Maltese.
Malta played a crucial role in World War II; the entire island was awarded the George Cross for its endurance under sustained Axis bombing.
The Blue Lagoon on Comino island is renowned for its brilliant turquoise waters and draws visitors from across Europe.
Maltese is the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet and is officially recognized as an EU language.
Malta joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2008.
The Knights of St. John ruled Malta from 1530 to 1798, building much of the fortified architecture that defines Valletta today.

funFacts: Luxembourg has one of the highest GDP per capita in the world, driven heavily by banking and finance.
Public transport (buses, trains, trams) throughout the entire country has been free for all riders since 2020.
Luxembourg is the only sovereign grand duchy left in the world today.
Luxembourgish, French, and German are all official languages, and most residents speak at least two of them fluently.
Luxembourg City's old quarters and fortifications, nicknamed the 'Gibraltar of the North' for their former defensive strength, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Luxembourg was a founding member of the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951, and today hosts major EU institutions including the Court of Justice of the European Union.
Roughly half of Luxembourg's workforce commutes in daily from France, Germany, and Belgium, giving it one of the highest shares of cross-border workers of any country.
Radio Luxembourg was one of Europe's most influential commercial radio stations in the mid-20th century, broadcasting pop music to listeners across the continent, including the UK.
Despite its small size, Luxembourg has its own wine-growing region along the Moselle River.

Andorra has no standing army and relies on France and Spain for defense.
Andorra has no airport or active passenger railway station; visitors arrive by road, usually via Barcelona or Toulouse.
Andorra, tucked high in the Pyrenees between France and Spain, is one of the smallest countries in Europe.
Catalan is the sole official language of Andorra, though French and Spanish are also widely spoken.
Andorra la Vella, the capital, is the highest-elevation capital city in Europe.
Andorra did not join the United Nations until 1993, despite its government tracing back to a 1278 charter.
Andorra's economy depends heavily on winter tourism, with ski resorts like Grandvalira among the largest in the Pyrenees.
Andorra has consistently ranked among the countries with the highest life expectancy in the world.
Andorra has one of the lowest standard VAT rates in Europe, part of why it is known as a duty-free shopping destination.

Liechtenstein is a constitutional monarchy ruled by the House of Liechtenstein, one of the few remaining European monarchies where the prince retains substantial political power.
The country has no airport of its own; most international travel goes through Zurich Airport in Switzerland.
At about 25 km long and 160 square kilometers, Liechtenstein is the sixth-smallest country in the world.
Liechtenstein abolished its army in 1868 and has remained neutral and without a military ever since.
It uses the Swiss franc as its currency and shares a customs union with Switzerland.
The country is divided into two regions, Oberland (upper) and Unterland (lower), each with its own distinct local dialect.
Liechtenstein became a sovereign state in 1806 after joining Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine.
Women in Liechtenstein were not granted the right to vote until 1984, making it one of the last countries in Europe to extend suffrage.
Vaduz Castle, perched on a hill above the capital, is the actual residence of the reigning prince, not just a museum or ceremonial building.

Land reclamation from the sea has expanded Monaco's territory by roughly 20% over the past century.
The Monte Carlo Casino, opened in 1863, helped establish Monaco's reputation as a glamorous resort destination and remains a city landmark.
Monaco is a full member of the United Nations despite having a population of under 40,000, among the smallest of any member state.

San Marino has never had a king; it is governed as a republic led by two Captains Regent who each serve six-month terms.
Despite covering only about 61 square kilometers, San Marino is one of the wealthiest countries in the world by GDP per capita.
San Marino's national football team once scored one of the fastest goals in World Cup qualifying history, after just 8.3 seconds, against England in 1993.
San Marino issues its own postage stamps and euro coins, popular with collectors worldwide despite not being an EU member.

The Vatican Library holds one of the oldest and most significant manuscript collections in the world.

funFacts: Lesotho is the only country in the world entirely above 1,000 meters in elevation, earning it the nickname 'Kingdom in the Sky'.
Lesotho is completely surrounded by South Africa, making it one of only three countries in the world (an 'enclave') entirely encircled by a single other nation.
Lesotho's economy depends heavily on textile manufacturing exports and remittances from citizens working in South Africa's mines.
The Maloti-Drakensberg mountain range is home to Afriski Mountain Resort, one of southern Africa's few ski destinations.
The Lesotho Highlands Water Project supplies water to South Africa's Gauteng region through a massive network of dams and tunnels, one of the largest water-transfer schemes in the world.
The Basotho blanket, a thick woolen blanket worn over the shoulders, is a defining part of national dress, often given as a gift to mark major life events.
Basotho ponies are a key form of transport in Lesotho's mountainous terrain, and pony-trekking has become a popular way for visitors to explore the highlands.
Thabana Ntlenyana, at 3,482 meters, is the highest point in southern Africa and lies within Lesotho.
Lesotho gained independence from Britain in 1966.
In the early 19th century, Moshoeshoe I united various Basotho clans and used skillful diplomacy to protect his kingdom from Zulu and Boer incursions.
ls.currencyNote: The Lesotho loti is pegged 1:1 to the South African rand, which also circulates as legal tender.

funFacts: Mali's medieval emperor Mansa Musa is often cited as the richest person in recorded history, his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca reportedly caused gold prices in Egypt to crash for over a decade due to the sheer amount he distributed.
Timbuktu was a legendary center of Islamic scholarship, home to hundreds of thousands of ancient manuscripts, some of which were smuggled to safety during a 2012 jihadist occupation.
The Great Mosque of Djenné, the largest mud-brick building in the world, is replastered annually by the local community in a communal festival event.
The Niger River sustains much of Mali's agriculture, flowing through the country in a great arc across the Sahel.
Mali gained independence from France in 1960.
The Dogon people of central Mali are known for their distinctive cliff-side villages and elaborate masked dances.
Malian musicians like Ali Farka Touré and Salif Keita brought the country's griot musical traditions to global audiences.

funFacts: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt - over 200 Nubian pyramids remain at Meroe, built by the ancient Kingdom of Kush.
Sudan is one of the world's largest producers of gum arabic, a key ingredient in soft drinks, candy, and cosmetics, sourced from acacia trees.
The ancient Kingdom of Kush, centered in what is now Sudan, once ruled over Egypt itself as the 25th Dynasty of pharaohs.
The Blue Nile and White Nile rivers meet at Khartoum, Sudan's capital, before flowing on as the Nile toward Egypt.
Sudan was Africa's largest country by area until South Sudan's secession in 2011 split off roughly a quarter of its territory.
Nuba wrestling, a traditional sport in Sudan's Nuba Mountains, has historically served as a major community and cultural event.
Port Sudan on the Red Sea has served as the country's main maritime gateway since it was built in the early 20th century to replace the older port of Suakin.
Sudan's Nubian pyramids at Meroe, though smaller than Egypt's, are far more numerous, with around 200 surviving structures.
sd.territorialNote: Sudan and South Sudan, which separated into two countries in 2011, continue to dispute the status of the oil-producing Abyei border region.

The Sudd, one of the world's largest freshwater wetlands, covers a vast area of South Sudan and was historically a major barrier to explorers trying to trace the source of the Nile.
South Sudan has more than 60 ethnic groups, with the Dinka and Nuer being the largest.
Traditional wrestling, especially among the Nuer and Dinka peoples, is one of South Sudan's most popular and culturally significant sports.
Oil accounts for the vast majority of South Sudan's government revenue, making it one of the most oil-dependent economies in the world.
Juba, the capital, has historically been poorly connected by paved roads to the rest of the country, reflecting the region's long isolation and underdevelopment.
South Sudan's national basketball team qualified for the 2024 Paris Olympics, its first-ever Olympic appearance, drawing international attention to the country's rising basketball talent.
The Boma-Badingilo landscape in South Sudan hosts one of the largest wild land-mammal migrations on Earth, rivaling the Serengeti's wildebeest migration.

funFacts: Chad is named after Lake Chad, once one of Africa's largest lakes, though it has shrunk by over 90% since the 1960s due to climate change and overuse.
A skull fossil found in Chad in 2001, nicknamed 'Toumaï' (Sahelanthropus tchadensis), is among the oldest known hominid fossils, estimated at nearly 7 million years old.
Chad is sometimes called the 'Dead Heart of Africa' because of its remote, landlocked location near the geographic center of the continent.
The Ennedi Plateau, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, contains dramatic sandstone formations and ancient rock art depicting a once-lush Sahara.
Chad is home to Zakouma National Park, known for its recovering elephant population after a severe poaching crisis in the 2000s.
N'Djamena, the capital, sits at the confluence of the Chari and Logone rivers near the border with Cameroon.
Chad has more than 200 ethnic groups and over 100 languages are spoken across the country, making it one of Africa's most linguistically diverse nations.
Lake Chad historically sat at the meeting point of four countries - Chad, Niger, Nigeria, and Cameroon - making it a major regional resource shared across borders.

Niger is home to the last remaining wild population of West African giraffes, found roaming freely outside protected areas near Niamey.
Niger is named after the Niger River, which flows through the southwestern part of the country.
The Sahara Desert covers more than three-quarters of Niger's territory.
The historic city of Agadez has a centuries-old mud-brick Grand Mosque that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Niger has one of the highest birth rates of any country in the world.
The W National Park, shared by Niger, Benin, and Burkina Faso, is named for the W-shaped bend of the Niger River within it and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Niger is a crossroads of Tuareg, Hausa, and Djerma-Songhai cultures, each with distinct languages and traditions.

The Batammariba people of Koutammakou are famous for their distinctive mud tower-houses (Tata Somba), recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape.
Togo is a narrow country, stretching about 540 km from north to south but only around 115 km at its widest point.
Lake Togo, a coastal lagoon connected to the Gulf of Guinea, is popular for watersports and supports local fishing communities.
Togo's national football team, the Hawks (Éperviers), qualified for the FIFA World Cup in 2006, their only appearance to date.
Lomé's Akodessawa Fetish Market is one of West Africa's largest traditional-medicine markets, reflecting the deep roots of Vodun (voodoo) in Togolese culture.
Togo was a German colony before World War I, then divided between Britain and France as League of Nations mandates after Germany's defeat.
Togo's capital, Lomé, sits right on the border with Ghana, and its central market has long been a major West African hub for textile trading.

The country's brutal civil war (1991-2002), fueled by control of diamond mines, inspired the term 'blood diamonds' and the 2006 film of that name.
Freetown, Sierra Leone's capital, was founded in 1792 as a settlement for freed and formerly enslaved people, giving the city its name.
Sierra Leone is home to Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary, a leading center for the rescue and rehabilitation of endangered chimpanzees.
Bunce Island off Sierra Leone's coast was a major departure point in the trans-Atlantic slave trade, with historical links to the Gullah communities of the southeastern United States.
Sierra Leone's rainforests and Western Area Peninsula beaches make it one of West Africa's most biodiverse coastal regions.
Sierra Leone holds some of the richest diamond and rutile mineral deposits in West Africa.
Krio, an English-based creole language, serves as Sierra Leone's lingua franca and is spoken by nearly the entire population as a first or second language.

Pico Cão Grande is a dramatic 663-meter volcanic plug that rises almost vertically from the rainforest, a striking landmark of the island of São Tomé.
The islands were uninhabited until Portuguese explorers arrived and settled them in the late 15th century.
São Tomé and Príncipe was once the world's largest producer of cocoa, in the early 20th century, and cocoa remains a key export today.
The country lies almost exactly on the Equator, with the small islet of Ilhéu das Rolas marking the equatorial line.
The islands are a biodiversity hotspot, home to bird species found nowhere else on Earth, including the São Tomé fiscal shrike and the dwarf olive ibis.
Portuguese is the official language, and a Portuguese-based creole called Forro is widely spoken across the islands.
Covering less than 1,000 square kilometers, São Tomé and Príncipe is one of the smallest countries in the world by land area.

The country was officially renamed from Swaziland to Eswatini in 2018 by royal decree, meaning 'land of the Swazis' in the Swazi language.
Eswatini is one of the smallest countries in Africa by area, landlocked between South Africa and Mozambique.
The annual Umhlanga (Reed Dance) ceremony, in which thousands of unmarried women participate, is one of the country's most important cultural traditions.
Eswatini has one of the highest HIV prevalence rates in the world, prompting major national public-health campaigns.
Mlilwane Wildlife Sanctuary was the country's first protected nature reserve and remains a major draw for visitors.
Sugar cane is among Eswatini's leading agricultural exports and a cornerstone of its economy.
Hlane Royal National Park is one of the best places in southern Africa to see lions and elephants in the wild.

Mauritius is often cited as one of Africa's most stable democracies and highest-income economies, built on sugar, textiles, tourism, and finance.
Mauritius was uninhabited until Dutch, then French, then British colonizers successively settled it, with British rule lasting from 1810 until independence in 1968.

Mauritius has no indigenous population; its people descend from waves of settlers, enslaved Africans, and indentured laborers from India and China, producing a notably multicultural, multilingual society.
Mauritian Creole, based on French, is the most widely spoken language in daily life, while English is the official language of government.
Mauritius is surrounded by one of the world's most extensive coral reef systems, supporting a major tourism and diving industry.
Sega music, with roots among enslaved Africans on the island, is Mauritius's traditional music and dance form.

Aldabra Atoll, a UNESCO site in Seychelles, hosts the world's largest population of giant tortoises, over 100,000 individuals.
Seychelles is Africa's smallest country by both population and land area, made up of 115 granite and coral islands.
Seychelles was uninhabited until French and later British settlers arrived in the 18th century, giving the islands a mixed Creole culture.
Seychellois Creole, derived from French, is one of the country's three official languages alongside English and French.
Nearly half of Seychelles' total land area is protected as national parks or nature reserves, among the highest proportions in the world.
Seychelles pioneered a 'debt-for-nature swap' and issued the world's first sovereign blue bond to finance marine conservation.
Early explorers were so struck by the coco de mer palms of Praslin's Valle de Mai that some nicknamed it a possible site of the Garden of Eden.

Chuuk Lagoon is one of the world's premier wreck-diving sites, home to dozens of Japanese ships sunk during a single US air raid in World War II.
Under a Compact of Free Association, citizens of the Federated States of Micronesia can live and work in the United States without a visa.
The US dollar is the official currency of the Federated States of Micronesia.
The FSM was part of the UN Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, administered by the United States, before gaining independence in 1986.

The Marshall Islands consists of 29 atolls and 5 islands scattered across more than 1,000 islets in the central Pacific.
The Marshall Islands gained full independence from the United States in 1986 under a Compact of Free Association that still closely ties the two countries.
Kwajalein Atoll has the largest lagoon of any atoll on Earth.
Traditional Marshallese navigators used 'stick charts,' woven maps of sticks and shells representing wave patterns, to navigate between islands without instruments.
The Marshall Islands is among the countries most threatened by rising sea levels, with much of its land barely above sea level.
